sources.name: Chronicle
sources.whatIsIt: Narrative accounts of events written by contemporaries  -  clergy, merchants, court servants.
prompts: Identify the author's religion, social position, and who they were writing for. A court servant sees very different things from a parish priest.
Chronicles are narrative accounts  -  they tell a story, which means they make choices about what to include and how to frame it.

Chronicles reflect the dominant narrative of their time, not a neutral record of events. A chronicle written under Elizabeth carries Protestant assumptions and frames Mary's reign as a dark interlude. One written under Mary presents Protestant reform as heresy. The political climate of composition shapes every choice of what to include and how to frame it.
Were they eyewitnesses, or writing from other accounts? Chroniclers frequently copied from each other and repeated rumour.
Often written years after events. Memory fades and the political climate changes  -  both shape what gets written.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was to blame for political instability?
examples.attribution: Richard Grafton, Chronicle entry for 1549, written in 1568
examples.excerpt: After these revolts were pacified, many lords and councillors, disliking the government of the Lord Protector, started to plot to replace him. Each lord and councillor went through London armed, and had their servants likewise armed. They assembled at the house of the Earl of Warwick [later Duke of Northumberland]. Then they published a proclamation against him containing the following charges. First, that through his malicious and evil government, the Lord Protector had caused all the recent unrest in the country. Second, he was ambitious and sought his own glory. Third, that he ignored the advice of the councillors. Fourth, that he told untruths about the council to the King.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view. Grafton puts Somerset's 'government' at the centre of the trouble and shows the council arming against him.

But Grafton wrote in 1568, nearly twenty years after the events. He was not an eyewitness, and chronicles are usually second or third hand accounts built from earlier writings and what people said happened.
After Somerset's fall in October 1549, Northumberland's council controlled the official record. They had every reason to blame Somerset to justify their coup.
Everything Grafton could read or hear about 1549 reflects the information the government allowed to be known at the time. He is repeating Northumberland's version, not delivering a neutral judgement.

The detail about councillors arming themselves may be real, but the framing is loaded. The source tells us as much about what Northumberland's council wanted people to believe as about who was actually to blame.
knowledge: On 'many lords and councillors disliking the government of the Lord Protector' - the Anti-Somerset faction was a real coalition of reformers and conservatives (Warwick, Wriothesley, Paget) who feared his sympathy for commoners had encouraged the 1549 unrest. The 'disliking' is accurate, but the framing makes it sound spontaneous when it was a coordinated political move.

On the lords going 'armed' through London - the events of October 1549 were a coup. Somerset took possession of Edward and called for loyal subjects to defend the King. The Council moved against him at Windsor. Grafton compresses a tense political crisis into one image.

On Somerset's blame for instability - the evidence suggests the 1552 treason charges against him were fabricated to remove him as a rival to Northumberland. The actual cause of his fall was factional politics, not the unrest itself.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was resistance and opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: Robert Parkyn, Narrative of the Reformation, 1553
examples.excerpt: Queen Mary was proclaimed at York on the 21st day of July and at Pontefract, Doncaster, Rotherham and many other market towns on the 22nd July, where everyone in all places in the north parts greatly rejoiced, making great fires, drinking wine and ale, praising God. But all such as were of heretical opinions, with bishops and priests having wives, did nothing rejoice, but began to be ashamed of themselves, for the common people would point them with fingers in places where they saw them. And in the beginning of September there were very few parish churches in Yorkshire, but mass was sung or said in Latin on the first Sunday of the said month.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view, showing joy in the north at Mary's accession rather than resistance.
Parkyn was a Yorkshire priest and firm supporter of Roman Catholicism. He had every reason to celebrate Mary's arrival and may well have seen what he wanted to see.

Chronicles like this are usually second or third hand for anything outside the writer's immediate parish. His claim about 'everyone in all places in the north parts' goes well beyond what one priest could actually know.
A Protestant observer watching the same crowds might have described them very differently.
The source is good evidence of northern Catholic enthusiasm for Mary, but it cannot be used to claim her accession was universally welcomed.
knowledge: On the joy in 'the north parts' - Mary's strongest power base was actually East Anglia. The widespread acclamation of her accession reflected commitment to hereditary succession under Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession, with most accepting Mary's right as the lawful heir.

On the celebrations - Northumberland's troops deserted to Mary and councillors broke ranks to declare for her. The whole Jane Grey affair collapsed in nine days. The popular reaction was real, but it was about legitimacy as much as religion.

On using 'the north parts' as evidence for the country - Edwardian Protestantism had taken hold most strongly in London, the south-east and East Anglia. The north and west had stayed more conservative. Parkyn's joy at York cannot stand for England as a whole.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was resistance and opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: Charles Wriothesley, Wriothesley's Chronicle, April 1554
examples.excerpt: On Sunday, a villainous event took place in Cheapside. A dead cat was hanged on the post of the gallows, dressed in cloth like the vestment of a priest at mass with crosses front and back. Its head was shaved, a bottle was nearby and between its front paws was a piece of paper like a consecrated wafer. It was taken to Bishop Bonner of London, who showed it to the audience attending the sermon at St. Paul's Cross. The lord mayor offered a reward to anyone naming the culprit. Inquiries were made and several persons were imprisoned under suspicion.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. Mock vestments hung on a dead cat in Cheapside is open Protestant mockery of the Catholic mass in the heart of London.
Wriothesley was a London chronicler with reformist sympathies. The incident probably stuck in his mind because it confirmed his own sense of what was happening in the capital.
Calling it a 'villainous event' is the official Marian framing. He records the regime's outrage even where his own sympathies might have been more mixed.
Chronicles are second or third hand for anywhere outside the writer's setting. London was the most reformed area in England, and what happened in Cheapside was not happening in Devon.
The source is strong evidence of London Protestant hostility to the Catholic restoration in 1554, but London was not England.
knowledge: On the mockery in Cheapside - London was the most Protestant area of England by 1554. Cheapside is in the heart of the City. This is exactly the kind of place where Protestant resistance was concentrated.

On open Protestant defiance - by early 1554 around 800 Protestants had already fled to Germany and Switzerland to escape the restoration. Those who stayed and were committed Protestants would express their hostility in incidents like this.

On reading this as nationwide resistance - in conservative areas like the south-west, parishioners were welcoming the return of Catholic worship. Most church records show Catholic restoration was accepted more readily than the earlier Edwardian Reformation had been.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was resistance and opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: Henry Machyn, diary, February 1555
examples.excerpt: The fourth day of February the bishop of London went into Newgate prison with other doctors to degrade Hooper and Rogers – sometime vicar of St Paul's. The same day was Rogers carried, between 10 and 11 o'clock, into Smithfield and burned for his critical opinions, with great company of the queen's guard. The fifth day of February between 5 and 6 in the morning, departed master Hooper to Gloucester and Saunders to Coventry, both to be burned.
provenance: On the surface this neither supports nor challenges the view. It is a flat factual record of the first Marian burning.
Machyn was a London merchant and a conservative Catholic. He records the event without praise or condemnation, which is itself revealing about how it was received.
His diary is one of the few non-official daily records of London life under Mary. The detail of times and names suggests genuine eyewitness or near-eyewitness knowledge.
Crucially he does not record crowds weeping or cheering. That absence is significant given what other ambassadors and chroniclers claim about public reaction.
The source is useful evidence of what happened and when, but says little directly about how Londoners actually felt.
knowledge: On 'Rogers was carried... and burned' - Rogers, a biblical translator, was the first of 284 Protestants burnt between 1555 and 1558. Choosing a high-profile figure first was a deliberate regime decision to make an example.

On the absence of crowd reaction in Machyn's account - other sources record large crowds at the burnings. Foxe presents them as sympathetic to the victims; some contemporaries report them attending as entertainment. Machyn's flat description cuts against both.

On the timing - Gardiner, who opposed the burnings as counter-productive, was still alive in February 1555. After his death in November 1555 the pace increased sharply under Cardinal Pole's direction.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary Tudor's government was weak?
examples.attribution: Charles Wriothesley, Wriothesley's Chronicle for 1554
examples.excerpt: On 1 February the Queen went to the Guildhall and declared to the audience the wicked plan of the traitor Wyatt, which was utterly to deprive her of her crown, and to ransack the city. She spoke so nobly, with so good spirit, and with so loud a voice, that all the people might hear her Majesty, and were comforted in their hearts with so sweet words which made them weep with joy to hear her Majesty speak. On 3 February the Queen appointed Lord William Howard to be Captain General, with the Lord Mayor, for the defence of the City.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of weakness, showing Mary rallying London personally during Wyatt's rebellion.
Wriothesley was a London chronicler writing soon after the events. He probably witnessed the speech or knew people who did, so the basic detail is likely accurate.
His framing of Wyatt as a 'traitor' and Mary speaking 'nobly' reflects the official line after the rebellion was crushed. Successful regimes shape how their crises are remembered.
The detail that 'all the people might hear her' is part of the bravery narrative being constructed around Mary's response to the crisis.
The source is good evidence of Mary's personal courage in that moment, but one successful speech cannot prove her government was strong overall.
knowledge: On Mary speaking 'so nobly' at the Guildhall - Mary refused her Council's advice to flee the city, and her speech personally secured Londoners' loyalty. The bravery and impact described here are factually borne out, not just chronicler praise.

On the rebellion - Wyatt had raised 3,000 men and reached the gates of London. Government troops under Norfolk had deserted to him, declaring 'We are all Englishmen!' Mary's speech was the turning point in a genuinely serious crisis.

On reading this as evidence of strong government overall - one successful speech in one moment does not prove general strength. The marriage that caused the rebellion was deeply unpopular, and the loss of Calais in 1558 came as a direct consequence of the Spanish alliance.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was widespread opposition to religious changes under Edward VI?
examples.attribution: Chronicle of Grey Friars of London (Catholic chronicle)
examples.excerpt: The 5th of September 1547 began the king's visitation at St Paul's, and all the images were pulled down; and the 9th day of the same month the said visitation was at St Bride's, and after that in various other parish churches; and so all images pulled down through all England at that time, and all churches new white-limed, with the commandments on the walls.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of opposition, suggesting smooth nationwide compliance with the removal of images.
The Grey Friars chronicle was written by London-based Catholic friars who watched these events with horror. Their hostility to the changes is the lens.
The phrase 'all images pulled down through all England' is impossible for any London friar to have known. He is generalising from what he saw in his own city.
Chronicles are second or third hand for events outside the writer's setting. London was the most heavily reformed area. Parishes far from the capital often did not comply nearly as quickly.
The source is good evidence for the visitation's impact at St Paul's and in the City of London. It cannot be used to claim nationwide compliance.
knowledge: On 'all images pulled down through all England' - de jure England was being made Protestant fast, but de facto compliance was patchy. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia.

On the iconoclasm at St Paul's - this is the centre of London, the most receptive area to reform. In Bishop Hooper's diocese of Gloucester, 171 of 311 clergymen could not even repeat the Ten Commandments. The pace of change varied enormously.

On the friars' framing of universal change - the rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary suggests traditional religion had retained popularity at the local level in most parts of the country. The friars' horror is genuine but unrepresentative.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Wyatt's rebellion was a serious threat to Mary?
examples.attribution: Charles Wriothesley, Chronicle of England, 1554
examples.excerpt: On 29 January the duke of Norfolk tried to attack Rochester castle, where the traitor Wyatt and his rebels lay, but he was forced to flee, and the rebels captured his artillery. On 1 February the queen went to Guildhall and declared to the audience the wicked plan of the traitor Wyatt, which was utterly to deprive her of her crown, and to ransack the city. She spoke so nobly, with so good spirit, and with so loud a voice, that all the people might hear her majesty, and were comforted in their hearts with so sweet words which made them weep with joy to hear her majesty speak. On 3 February Wyatt's army reached London Bridge. On 7 February the earl of Pembroke gathered the royal army at Charing Cross near the city, but Wyatt and some rebels avoided them and got close to the city, where they were captured.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The royal commander defeated and the rebels capturing his artillery is a serious military reverse.
Wriothesley was a London chronicler with access to court news. The detail of Norfolk's flight and the lost artillery is specific and probably accurate.
He uses 'the traitor Wyatt' framing, the official line after the rebellion was crushed. But the underlying military facts cannot be hidden behind that language.
Chronicles tend to focus on dramatic reverses because they make better stories. Norfolk's defeat is exactly the kind of incident that gets remembered.
The source is strong evidence of the immediate military danger to Mary's regime in late January 1554, before her Guildhall speech rallied London.
knowledge: On Norfolk forced to flee and the rebels capturing his artillery - government troops under Norfolk deserted to Wyatt's side, declaring 'We are all Englishmen!' The military reverse Wriothesley describes is real and serious.
On Wyatt's threat - he raised 3,000 men and reached the gates of London. The rebellion was only defeated after Mary's Guildhall speech secured Londoners' loyalty and the city gates remained shut.

On reading the rebellion as catastrophically dangerous - only one of the four planned uprisings actually rose. The discovery of the plot forced winter timing, when fewer peasants would join. Rochester was a moment in a rebellion ultimately undone by its own discovery.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Wyatt's rebellion was a serious threat to Mary?
examples.attribution: John Proctor, A History of Wyatt's Rebellion, 1554 [government-commissioned account]
examples.excerpt: Wyatt, proceeding in his detestable purpose, armed himself and as many as he could. And, considering that the restoring of the newly-forged religion was not a cause general enough to attract all sorts to support him, he determined to speak no word of religion, but to make the colour of his commotion only to withstand strangers and advance liberty.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view by making Wyatt look manipulative and politically weak rather than militarily dangerous.
Proctor's history was commissioned by Mary's government after the rebellion. Its job is to explain and justify the regime's view of what happened.

The argument that Wyatt hid his real Protestant motives is exactly what the government wanted people to believe. It turns the rebellion into a religious plot rather than a popular protest against the Spanish marriage.
'Detestable purpose' and 'newly-forged religion' are loaded language. This is not a neutral account, it is official propaganda dressed as history.
The source tells us what Mary's regime needed people to believe about Wyatt's motives, not what those motives actually were.
knowledge: On 'newly-forged religion was not a cause general enough... he determined to speak no word of religion' - Proctor is right that the rebellion's manifestos focused on the Spanish marriage. But the timing immediately followed Mary's marriage announcement, and Wyatt had been loyal during the Jane Grey affair. The marriage looks like the real trigger, not a smokescreen.

On Wyatt as manipulative - Proctor was the government's chronicler and would be 'unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip'. Framing Wyatt as hiding his real Protestant motive lets the regime avoid admitting the unpopularity of the marriage.

On the rebellion's threat - 3,000 men, Norfolk's troops defecting, the gates of London reached. The rebellion was a serious threat in scale and reach, regardless of how Proctor wants to frame its motives.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that ambition was the main cause of Somerset's downfall?
examples.attribution: A chronicle outlines the charges against Somerset, October 1549
examples.excerpt: First that through his malicious and evil government, the Lord Protector had caused all the recent unrest in the country. Second, he was ambitious and sought his own glory. Third, that he had ignored the advice of his councillors.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The charges blame Somerset for the unrest and accuse him of ambition.
These charges were drafted by Northumberland's council after the coup against Somerset. They are not a neutral assessment, they are the justification for the coup.
Northumberland's regime needed Somerset's government to look like the cause of all the trouble. That framing made the coup look necessary rather than self-interested.
Even where it ends up written into a chronicle, this is essentially official propaganda from the new regime being recorded as if it were a neutral account.
The source tells us how the post-coup council needed Somerset's fall to be understood, not whether his ambition was actually the main cause of his downfall.
knowledge: On 'malicious and evil government... caused all the recent unrest' - the 1549 unrest covered over 25 counties, the most widespread of the Tudor period. The deeper causes were inflation, debasement, population pressure (rising from 2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551), and enclosure, none of which Somerset created.

On Somerset being 'ambitious' - the evidence suggests the 1552 treason charges against him were fabricated to remove him as a rival to Northumberland. The 'ambition' charge was the political case the coup needed to make, not a measured judgement.

On 'he had ignored the advice of his councillors' - Paget had warned Somerset in July 1549 that the King's subjects were 'out of all discipline'. There was real contemporary frustration with his approach, but turning that into formal treason charges was a political act.

sources.name: Ambassador Report
sources.whatIsIt: Letters sent by foreign ambassadors to their governments, reporting on English politics and court affairs.
prompts: The ambassador's nationality determines their priorities. A Spanish ambassador focuses on Habsburg interests; a Venetian on trade and European power. There is no neutral observer.
Diplomatic dispatches are written to inform and impress. Admitting uncertainty or missing key events would damage their career.
Ambassadors relied on local informants with their own agendas. 'Popular discontent' may reflect one contact's anxiety, not general opinion.
Foreign observers often misread English political culture. Being an outsider does not make you more objective.
Crises are over-reported, stability is under-reported. Ambassadors needed to seem useful to their masters.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the succession never seriously threatened political stability?
examples.attribution: Christophe d'Assonleville, letter to King Philip of Spain, 7 November 1558
examples.excerpt: As the Queen continues to be ill, the Privy Council spoke to her yesterday in order to persuade her to declare the Lady Elizabeth her heir. Her Majesty agreed; and the Council today will visit the Lady Elizabeth and inform her that the Queen is willing that she should succeed in the event of her own death, but that she asks two things of her: one that she will maintain the old religion as the Queen restored it; and the other that she will pay the Queen's debts.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view, showing a smooth and orderly succession arrangement at the end of Mary's reign.
D'Assonleville was a Spanish ambassador with strong Habsburg interests in the succession going cleanly to Elizabeth, who Philip then hoped to marry.
His report is short and matter-of-fact. He has no incentive to dramatise problems here, because the outcome suited Spain.
Ambassadors learn what their court contacts choose to tell them. He is repeating the version of events the Council wanted Spain to receive.
The source supports the view that the 1558 transition was handled without serious instability, but the Spanish ambassador's interest in that being the story should be borne in mind.
knowledge: On the Council persuading Mary to declare Elizabeth - the succession did pass peacefully to Elizabeth despite Catholic concerns about her legitimacy. Philip of Spain, who could have pressed a Catholic claim, chose not to.

On the orderly handover - Mary died on 17 November 1558. Cardinal Pole died the same day, leaving the Church without an Archbishop. England had lost Calais. Beneath d'Assonleville's tidy report was an inherited crisis.

On reading this as 'no serious threat' - Mary's failure to produce an heir had left Catholic restoration vulnerable from the start. Mary Queen of Scots had a strong alternative claim. The peaceful succession in November did not mean the succession question had never threatened stability.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was to blame for political instability?
examples.attribution: Francis Bourgoyne, letter to John Calvin, 22 January 1552
examples.excerpt: Somerset was the head of a conspiracy against the whole Council, and more particularly against the Duke of Northumberland, whom Somerset pursued with a deadly hatred, since Northumberland had been foremost among those who deprived him of the rank of Lord Protector. Somerset obtained some supporters from among the Council itself. They agreed that Northumberland should be murdered and they should take over the government of the kingdom. Somerset should lead the government, or even be restored to the office of Protector.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view that Somerset was to blame for the political instability of 1551-52.
Bourgoyne was a French Protestant pastor writing to Calvin in Geneva. He was not in England witnessing events, he was reporting English news at distance.
His information came from the English Protestant network, which by 1552 was aligned with Northumberland's regime. He is repeating their framing.
'Deadly hatred' is the language of the post-coup case against Somerset. It reflects the version Northumberland's council was putting out.
The source tells us what the Protestant network around Northumberland wanted Calvin to believe about Somerset, not whether Somerset was actually conspiring.
knowledge: On Somerset 'the head of a conspiracy against the whole Council' - Somerset had been arrested in October 1549. The 1552 case was a second prosecution after his initial release. The evidence suggests the charges were fabricated to remove him as Northumberland's rival.

On 'deadly hatred' against Northumberland - Somerset had been allowed back onto the Council in the hope he would support Northumberland. The relationship broke down because Northumberland saw him as a continuing threat, not because Somerset launched a genuine conspiracy.

On reading Calvin's correspondent as a guide to English politics - Bourgoyne is reporting what the English Protestant network told him. By 1552 that network was aligned with Northumberland's regime, which needed Somerset to look conspiratorial.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, report to Philip of Spain, 5 February 1555 [Imperial/Spanish ambassador]
examples.excerpt: The people of London are murmuring about the cruel enforcement of the recent acts of Parliament against heresy which has now begun, as shown publicly when a certain Rogers was burnt yesterday. Some of the onlookers wept. Others prayed to God to give them strength, persistence, and patience to bear the pain and not to convert back to Catholicism. Others gathered the ashes and bones and wrapped them up in paper to preserve them. Yet others threatened the bishops. The haste with which the bishops have proceeded in this matter may well cause a revolt. If the people got the upper hand, not only would the cause of religion be again menaced, but the persons of your Majesty and the Queen might be in peril.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view, suggesting the burnings were creating real public anger in London.
Renard was a Spanish ambassador with a vested interest in Mary's regime succeeding. He has no reason to invent opposition.
But Renard's job was to flag risks to his masters in Brussels. He tended to dramatise threats because that was what kept him useful.
'May well cause a revolt' is his speculation, not a fact. His informants were close to him in London. He was not watching the burnings in other parts of the country.
The source is good evidence of London hostility to the first burnings in early 1555. The talk of 'revolt' reflects Renard's instinct to flag danger, not necessarily reality.
knowledge: On 'the people of London are murmuring' - the burnings were concentrated in London, Kent and Essex, the Protestant strongholds. Renard's report of London anger matches the geographical reality of where the burnings were happening.
On 'may well cause a revolt' - no popular revolt followed. The burnings continued for nearly three more years, ending only with Mary's death in 1558. Renard's predicted danger never materialised.

On the early-stage reaction - Renard is writing about the first major burning (John Rogers, 4 February 1555). Gardiner was still alive and opposed the burnings as counter-productive. Mary herself had already advised the Council in December 1554 to act 'without rashness', showing regime awareness of the risk.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary Tudor's government was weak?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, letter to Charles V, 18 September 1554 [Imperial/Spanish ambassador]
examples.excerpt: No attention is paid to the law; the Queen and her council are neither respected nor obeyed nor feared. The people say that King Philip is not going to employ Englishmen, though he agreed to do so in the marriage treaty. They (the people) say he is sending for 10000 Germans and 10000 Spaniards to land in this country. They also say that monasteries will be set up again and that the Pope will control religious affairs. They proclaim that they (the people) are to be enslaved, for the Queen is a Spanish woman at heart and thinks nothing of Englishmen.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of weakness.
Renard's job was to flag problems for Philip and the Emperor. Crises were over-reported in his dispatches because that was what kept him useful.
'The people say' covers his London contacts, who were anxious about the Spanish marriage. It is not a measured assessment of national opinion.
He had personal influence over Mary and reasons to argue that her regime needed continued Spanish support. Painting things as bleak helped that case.
The source is evidence of Renard's view of the autumn 1554 mood. It is not a reliable measure of how weak Mary's government actually was.
knowledge: On 'neither respected nor obeyed nor feared' - Mary had defeated the Jane Grey coup in nine days, suppressed Wyatt's Rebellion personally, and negotiated a marriage treaty that significantly restricted Philip's power. Her record by autumn 1554 cuts against Renard's bleak framing.

On 'King Philip is not going to employ Englishmen' - the marriage treaty explicitly forbade Spaniards holding office in England. Mary kept total control of all offices, lands and revenues. The popular rumour Renard reports was unfounded.

On the wider regime - Mary streamlined the Council and her inner council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign' and 'successfully carried out her wishes'. Renard's snapshot of one moment of anxiety is not the whole picture.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Wyatt's rebellion was a serious threat to Mary?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, dispatch, 27 January 1554 [Imperial/Spanish ambassador]
examples.excerpt: Wyatt's men have rebelled in Kent, proclaiming that they will not consent to a foreign marriage and that every good Englishman ought to help them fight the Spaniards. Although the rebels use the foreign marriage as an excuse, like Carew, their real causes are religion and to favour Elizabeth. It is said that the rebellion is spreading. We hear news that the French and Scots are hastily fitting out ships and raising troops to aid the rebels. We hear the king of Denmark is joining in, hoping to marry Elizabeth to his son or brother.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of a serious threat. Renard reports Kent in rebellion and warns of religion and Elizabeth as the real motives behind the stated complaint against the Spanish marriage.

Renard was writing from the middle of the Spanish contingent at court, who were genuinely frightened by Wyatt's advance on London. The dispatch reflects their anxieties, and he was asking Charles V for help in the same letters.

He had every reason to recast the rebellion as religious and pro-Elizabeth. That framing made the rebels look illegitimate and helped defend the Spanish marriage, which was the source of his own influence.

The hedging language gives him away. 'It is said' and 'we hear news' show he is passing on court gossip rather than verified intelligence. The escalating list of France, Scots, and even the King of Denmark joining in reads as the hyperbole of a frightened ambassador, not a measured report.
The source is genuine evidence of the alarm inside the Spanish bubble at court in late January 1554, not a reliable measure of the rebels' real motives or the rebellion's actual scale.
knowledge: On 'Wyatt's men have rebelled in Kent' - the rebellion raised 3,000 men and reached the gates of London. Government troops under Norfolk deserted to join the rebels, declaring 'We are all Englishmen!' Renard's alarm is not overstated.

On 'their real causes are religion and to favour Elizabeth' - the rebellion's timing immediately followed Mary's marriage proposal in Parliament, and Wyatt had been loyal to Mary during the Jane Grey affair. He only turned after the marriage was announced. Religion is the convenient reading, not the most likely cause.

On Renard's framing - Proctor's government-commissioned history also blamed religion, exactly because the regime could not afford to admit popular opposition to Philip. The Spanish ambassador and the regime's chronicler reach the same conclusion for the same reasons.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary Tudor's government was weak?
examples.attribution: The Venetian ambassador, report to the Senate of Venice, 1557
examples.excerpt: She is not only brave and valiant, but so courageous and resolute that neither in adversity nor peril did she ever display cowardice, maintaining always a wonderful grandeur and dignity, knowing what suits the dignity of a sovereign as well as any of her experienced councillors. In government and public affairs she is compelled (being of a sex which cannot suitably take more than a moderate part in them) to refer many matters to her councillors and ministers. The truth is that knowing the divisions among them, her Majesty, so as not to be deceived, has ordered that Cardinal Pole should hear and have everything referred to him since she trusts him and distrusts almost all others.
provenance: On the surface this both supports and challenges the view. It praises Mary's courage but says she relies heavily on her councillors.
The Venetian ambassador had no direct stake in English politics. Venice valued accurate information for diplomatic decisions in the Mediterranean.
The professional and measured tone is the source's biggest danger. Calm prose makes it sound reliable, but the ambassador is still reporting court gossip and surface impressions.
The line about Mary being 'compelled' to refer to her councillors reflects assumptions about female rule shared across Europe in the 1550s. It is interpretation, not fact.
The source gives a balanced contemporary judgement on Mary's personal qualities, but it cannot tell us how her government was actually performing day to day.
knowledge: On Mary 'compelled... to refer matters to her councillors' - Mary did rely on her Council, but she streamlined it (casual councillors excluded from key committees in 1554; inner council established in 1555). The Council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign'.

On Mary's 'courageous and resolute' character - this matches her refusal to flee London during Wyatt's Rebellion, her personal Guildhall speech, and her willingness to push through Catholic restoration despite Council resistance. The personal qualities described are not just praise.

On the wider judgement - Mary 'in practice demonstrated that a woman could govern effectively'. She streamlined the Privy Council, passed major religious legislation, managed marriage negotiations, and suppressed Wyatt's Rebellion.

sources.name: Government Records
sources.whatIsIt: Documents produced by royal government  -  Acts of the Privy Council, royal proclamations, parliamentary statutes.
prompts: Whoever dominated the council controlled what got recorded. Somerset's arrest was written down by the men who arrested him.
Records decisions, not the arguments and deals behind them. The real politics happened before the clerk picked up his pen.
A proclamation shows what the government intended, not what actually happened. Check local sources to see if it was enforced.
If something had to be proclaimed, it probably wasn't happening naturally on its own.
Official records speak in the language of authority  -  they tell us how the government wanted its actions to appear, not the full reality.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the succession never seriously threatened political stability?
examples.attribution: The Privy Council, letter to Mary Tudor, 9 July 1553
examples.excerpt: We advise you that our Sovereign Lady Queen Jane is possessed of the crown, not only by good order of old ancient records of this realm, but also by the late King Edward's letters signed with his own hand and sealed with the Great Seal of England, with nobles, councillors and judges agreeing to these letters. We must remind you that owing to the divorce between King Henry VIII and your mother, in accordance with the law of God and confirmed by the acts of parliament [1534, 1537], you are illegitimate and unable to inherit the crown.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view of an orderly succession through Jane, framed in legal language.
The letter is dated 9 July, two days before the Council switched sides and proclaimed Mary. By 19 July they had all sworn loyalty to Mary instead.
This is the document the Council needed Mary to receive to legitimise Jane. It reflects the version of authority they were trying to enforce in that moment.
'Good order of old ancient records' is doing a lot of work to disguise the fact that Edward's Devise was on shaky legal ground.
The source tells us what Northumberland's regime needed to be true about the succession, not whether the succession was genuinely under their control.
knowledge: On 'our Sovereign Lady, Queen Jane is invested and possessed' - the Council had proclaimed Jane on 10 July, but by 19 July they had all switched sides and sworn loyalty to Mary. The 'invested and possessed' framing collapsed in nine days.

On Edward's 'letters signed with his own hand' - the Devise had no legal basis and went against Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession. Most people believed in hereditary succession as divinely ordained. The Council's legal language could not overcome that.

On reading this as evidence of a serious succession threat - Mary's accession was widely accepted, Northumberland's troops deserted, and the principle of hereditary succession was reinforced. The threat was contained because the Devise had no popular legitimacy.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: Mary Tudor to the Privy Council, December 1554
examples.excerpt: Touching punishment of heretics, we thinketh it ought to be done without rashness, not failing in the meanwhile to do justice to such as by learning would seem to deceive the simple. And the rest so to be used that the people might well perceive them not to be condemned without just oration, whereby they shall both understand the truth and beware to do the like. And especially within London I would wish none to be burnt without some of the Council's presence and – both there and everywhere – good sermons at the same.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view that the burnings were creating uncontrolled opposition. Mary herself is calling for restraint and managed publicity.
This is Mary's private instruction to her Council. It shows the regime knew the politics of the burnings were sensitive.
The insistence that Council members must attend executions in London suggests they understood London as a particular flashpoint.
The call for 'good sermons' alongside the burnings is propaganda awareness. They knew the executions alone might create the wrong impression.
The source is strong evidence that Mary herself was conscious of opposition. It does not show how successful her precautions actually were on the ground.
knowledge: On 'without rashness' - this came just before the burnings began (John Rogers, February 1555). The Council's awareness of risk matches Renard's later report of London murmuring.

On Council members attending in London - London was the centre of Protestant resistance and the geographical heart of where the burnings were concentrated. The Council understood London as the specific flashpoint Mary identifies.

On reading Mary's caution as evidence the burnings did not create opposition - Gardiner himself opposed the burnings as 'counter-productive'. After his death in November 1555 the pace increased sharply under Pole. The careful instructions here did not prevent the regime from creating Foxe's martyrs.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the succession never seriously threatened political stability?
examples.attribution: Mary I, last will and testament, 28 October 1558
examples.excerpt: My will was written when I thought I was pregnant, leaving the crown to my children ruled by my dearest husband if underage. As I have no heir, I wish my successor under my father's will and Act to fulfil my will by funding religious houses and a hospital. To her I leave my subjects' love for peaceful government and advancing God's glory. My dearest husband shall no longer rule this realm, but my legal successor shall. I beg His Majesty to remember my great love and humble duty to him, and be a powerful friend to my successor, my country and its subjects.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of a serious succession crisis, showing Mary preparing for a lawful transition at the end of her reign.
This is Mary's revision of her earlier will, made when she knew she was dying. The acknowledgement 'as I have no heir' comes very late.
The original will was written assuming pregnancy. That delay in facing the reality of the succession itself created political instability throughout her reign.
The reference to her father's 'will and Act' sidesteps the difficult question of whether Elizabeth is named as heir. It defers the answer.
The source shows how the regime handled the succession at the last moment, but says nothing about how stable the succession had been throughout Mary's reign.
knowledge: On 'as I have no heir' - this is Mary acknowledging the structural failure of her reign at the last moment. Her phantom pregnancy in 1555 had raised hopes that were quickly dashed, and Philip had largely abandoned England after 1555.

On 'my successor under my father's will and Act' - Mary will not name Elizabeth directly. Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate, due to the Pope's refusal of Henry VIII's divorce. Mary's reference to her father's will sidesteps that uncomfortable truth.

On reading this as 'stable transition' - the succession did pass peacefully to Elizabeth, but she inherited an immediate Catholic challenge to her legitimacy and a country weakened by war and debt. The peaceful handover does not mean the succession had not been an instability throughout Mary's reign.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was responsible for his own downfall?
examples.attribution: William Paget, letter to Protector Somerset, 7 July 1549
examples.excerpt: I told your grace the truth and was not believed. The king's subjects are out of all discipline, out of obedience, caring neither for protector nor king. And what is the cause? Your own softness? Your intention to be good to the poor? Consider, I beseech you most humbly, that society in a realm is maintained by means of religion and law. The use of the old religion is forbidden by a law, and the use of the new is not yet embraced by eleven out of twelve parts of the realm. As for the law, the foot takes on him the part of the head, and the common people are behaving like a king.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view that Somerset was responsible for the situation.
Paget was a senior councillor and close adviser to Somerset, writing in the middle of the 1549 risings. This is contemporary criticism from within Somerset's own circle.
He had warned Somerset earlier and was now reminding him of it. His tone reflects frustration and the desire to shape policy in the moment.
Paget was politically aligned with the conservatives. His framing of 'softness' reflects a specific position on how the government should have responded to social unrest.
The source is genuine evidence of contemporary criticism of Somerset from within his own council, but it is partisan advice and not a neutral judgement.
knowledge: On 'the king's subjects are out of all discipline' - 1549 saw the most widespread unrest of the Tudor period, over 25 counties. Paget's alarm matches the scale of the actual crisis.

On 'what is the cause? Your own softness?' - Somerset had earned a reputation as the 'Good Duke' through the Hales enclosure commission and his apparent sympathy for the commons. The Anti-Somerset faction blamed this sympathy for encouraging the unrest. Paget reflects that view directly.

On reading this as proof Somerset caused the unrest - the deeper causes were structural: inflation, debasement, population pressure rising from 2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551, enclosure, and bad harvests. Somerset's softness made him a target for blame, but he did not create these forces.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was responsible for his own downfall?
examples.attribution: Privy Council charges against the Duke of Somerset, 6 October 1549
examples.excerpt: The members of the king's majesty's Privy Council, considering among themselves the great rebellion of the people in various parts of the realm and the great slaughter and shedding of blood that has lately happened. The great disobedience remaining among the king's subjects consider that if speedy remedy is not provided, both his majesty's royal person and the whole state might be brought into peril. And remembering that this and other great disorders had proceeded from the ill government of the lord protector [Somerset]. The lord protector, who being spoken to many times in open council and privately, has not only refused to give ear to their advisers, but also deciding to follow his own fantasies from which all the said disorders and mischiefs have arisen.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view that Somerset's government caused the unrest.
These charges were drafted by the council that was overthrowing Somerset. They are the justification for the coup, not a neutral account.
The framing of 'ill government of the lord protector' reflects the information Northumberland's faction allowed to be known at the time.
The charges had to argue Somerset was uniquely dangerous to justify removing the Protector. Whatever his actual record, the charges had to make the strongest case.
The source tells us how the post-coup government needed Somerset's downfall to be understood, not whether he was truly to blame.
knowledge: On 'great disobedience remaining among the king's subjects' - 1549 saw unrest in over 25 counties, including Kett's 16,000 rebels at Norwich and the Western Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall. The unrest was real and serious.

On 'ill government of the lord protector' - the Anti-Somerset faction (Warwick, Wriothesley, Paget) needed this framing to justify the coup. The evidence suggests the 1552 treason charges against Somerset were fabricated. The October 1549 charges were the opening salvo of the same political process.

On underlying causes - inflation, debasement, population pressure and enclosure were European-wide problems Somerset did not create. The Vagrancy Act of 1547, with slavery as punishment, reflected fear rather than effective policy. These were structural failings, not personal ones.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that female rule was a serious problem in the 1550s?
examples.attribution: Act for the Marriage of Queen Mary to Philip of Spain, 1554
examples.excerpt: This treaty greatly honours and benefits England. The prince shall enjoy, jointly, the style and honour of king. He shall happily help administer England, preserving its rights, laws, privileges and customs. The Queen shall have total control of all offices, lands and revenues, and grant them to natural born Englishmen. Sincere friendship with Spain will be happily established forever, God willing, to benefit their successors. Should no children be born and the queen die before him, he shall accept the lawful heir. The prince shall take no jewels abroad, nor ships, guns or supplies. He shall renew defences of the realm. By this marriage, England shall not be entangled in war, and the prince shall observe England's peace with France.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view, presenting a balanced marriage that protects English sovereignty.
This is a Parliamentary statute drafted to reassure English elites worried about the Spanish marriage.
The very fact that all these restrictions had to be written into law shows how deep the worry was about female rule and a foreign king.
'Shall happily help administer' is reassurance language. Acts of Parliament are political documents, not neutral descriptions of how the marriage would actually work.
The source is strong evidence of how Mary's government tried to manage the political problem of her marriage. The size of the reassurance package itself reveals the scale of the underlying concern.
knowledge: On 'shall happily help administer England, preserving its rights' - the treaty was the product of careful negotiation by Paget. Philip was named King but had no power in his own right. The treaty's restrictions (no Spaniards in office, no claim after Mary's death, no involvement in Spain's wars) were largely respected.

On 'the Queen shall have total control of all offices' - this was a real protection of English sovereignty. The marriage still triggered Wyatt's Rebellion in January 1554, but the rebellion was defeated and Mary proceeded with the marriage on these terms.

On the marriage as evidence of the female rule problem - the elaborate treaty was needed because of anxieties about female rule. But Mary 'in practice demonstrated that a woman could govern effectively' - the structural problem was managed by the treaty, not exposed by it.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was widespread opposition to religious changes under Edward VI?
examples.attribution: An Act for the abolition and putting away of images and various books, 1549
examples.excerpt: The king has issued through Parliament a uniform, quiet and godly order of service called the Book of Common Prayer, which contains nothing but the pure word of God. However, alongside it are still practised corrupt, untrue and superstitious ceremonies, which allow some to attack the order and meaning of the Prayer Book and encourage great diversity of opinion. Therefore, it is ordered that all books used for the old mass be abolished, and any images of stone, timber or marble be defaced and destroyed.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view of opposition, since the Act admits Catholic practices were continuing despite the new Prayer Book.
The Act describes the religious changes as 'uniform, quiet and godly' but then has to explain why further legislation is needed.
That contradiction is the source's most useful feature. The government was forced to admit non-compliance even while claiming the new order was already settled.
'Corrupt, untrue and superstitious' is the official Protestant framing of what most parishes were still doing. It does not mean those practices were unpopular with parishioners.
The source is strong evidence that Protestant reform was running into significant continuing resistance in parishes across the country in 1549.
knowledge: On 'corrupt, untrue and superstitious ceremonies' continuing - the 1549 Prayer Book was a deliberate compromise so vague on the Eucharist that it 'pleased nobody'. Its ambiguity prompted the Western Rebellion in early 1549.

On the Act admitting non-compliance - at parish level compliance was 'patchy and often superficial'. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes except in London, the south-east and East Anglia. Many parishes removed images when required but continued private Catholic devotion.

On reading this as widespread opposition - 1549 also saw 25 counties in unrest. The Western Rebellion of that year was triggered specifically by the First Prayer Book. The Act's concern about continuing Catholic practice and the religious rebellion were happening at the same moment.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that enclosure was the most important cause of unrest in 1549?
examples.attribution: Protector Somerset, letter to Philip Hoby, 24 August 1549
examples.excerpt: Some rebels wish to pull down enclosures and parks; some want to recover their common land; others pretend religion is their motive. A number want to rule for a time, and do as gentlemen have done, and indeed all have a great hatred of gentlemen and regard them as their enemies. The ruffians among them, and the soldiers, who are the leaders, look for loot. So the rebellions are nothing more than a plague and fury among the vilest and worst sort of men.
provenance: On the surface this names multiple rebel motives - enclosure, common land, religion, social ambition, loot - which acknowledges that the 1549 unrest had several causes. The categorisation itself is more revealing than Somerset intends.

Somerset is the most senior figure in the regime, writing about rebellions that have undermined his own authority. By 24 August 1549 he is preparing the military response. The letter is a defence of his record, not a neutral analysis.

'others pretend religion is their motive' - Somerset cannot admit the religious cause because the First Prayer Book was his own settlement. Acknowledging that it had triggered the Western Rebellion would be acknowledging his own policy failure.

'all have a great hatred of gentlemen' is a real observation, but Somerset pivots immediately to blaming the rebels' character ('ruffians', 'soldiers', 'look for loot') rather than the conditions his commissions had encouraged.

The closing line - 'nothing more than a plague and fury among the vilest and worst sort of men' - strips dignity from the rebels entirely. The contempt is the regime's justification for the massacres it was about to unleash.
knowledge: On 'wish to pull down enclosures and parks' - Kett's 16,000 rebels in Norfolk gathered explicitly around enclosure and rents. In Norwich, 6% of the population owned 60% of the land. The grievance Somerset acknowledges first was real and acute.

On 'others pretend religion is their motive' - this dismisses the Western Rebellion, whose demands were almost entirely religious and triggered by the First Book of Common Prayer. Cornish rebels said the new service was 'like a Christmas game' and demanded the restoration of the Six Articles.

On 'great hatred of gentlemen' - Lord Sheffield was beaten to death by Kett's rebels at Norwich; Western rebels chanted 'Kill all the gentlemen!' at Bodmin. The hatred Somerset describes was real, but it was a symptom of structural inequality, not loot-seeking by 'ruffians'.

On 'a plague and fury among the vilest and worst sort of men' - the suppression that followed killed 3,000 at Dussindale (Kett) and over 3,000 in the Western Rebellion. The class contempt in Somerset's letter is the regime's framing of the violence it was about to use.

examples.paper: Guide Source Practice / Y107 past papers
examples.question: How far do they support the view that the introduction of Protestantism under Edward VI was difficult?
examples.attribution: Second Act of Uniformity, 1552
examples.excerpt: In spite of the introduction of the First Common Prayer Book by Parliament, a great number of people in this realm wilfully and damnably refuse to come to their parish churches on Sundays and holy days. In future those who are absent shall be punished by the Church courts. The First Common Prayer Book has produced doubts about the form of worship, so the King has ordered a Second Book of Common Prayer to replace it. Anyone who uses another form of worship shall be imprisoned for six months.
provenance: On the surface this is the government admitting in its own legislation that the First Prayer Book had failed. The Act itself is the evidence.

'wilfully and damnably refuse' uses theological language, not merely legal language. Calling non-attendance 'damnable' treats it as a sin against God, not just a breach of statute. The regime is escalating its rhetoric.
'doubts about the form of worship' reframes what had been a deliberate feature of the 1549 Prayer Book (its compromise wording on the Eucharist) as a failure that requires replacement.
The six months' imprisonment penalty shows how far the regime had moved by 1552. The First Act of Uniformity had no real enforcement teeth; the Second adds them.

Acts of Parliament are official statements of what the regime wants to be true. The fact that this Act is admitting widespread non-compliance is what makes it unusually useful evidence - it is the government against itself.
knowledge: On 'wilfully and damnably refuse to come' - the lack of punishment under the First Act had encouraged non-conformity. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia. The regime is admitting the problem its own first settlement created.
On 'six months' imprisonment' - the Second Act tightened enforcement, but Edward died in July 1553, only months after it took effect. The policy had no time to bed in before Mary reversed it.

On the lay-non-compliance focus - Bishop Hooper's visitations of Gloucester found 171 of 311 clergymen could not repeat the Ten Commandments. Clerical resistance was as much an obstacle as lay non-attendance. The Act could legislate against parishioners but not against priestly ignorance.

On reading this as evidence Protestantism was difficult - the rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary in 1553-54 confirms the Act's admission was understated. Traditional religion had retained popularity. The 1552 Act was tightening enforcement on a country that mostly had not converted.

sources.name: Legal Records
sources.whatIsIt: Court proceedings, attainders, and execution records  -  including the Seymour attainders and Marian heresy trials.
prompts: Charges were constructed by political enemies. Read them as evidence of what those enemies needed people to believe.
Tudor treason trials confirmed outcomes already decided. Parliamentary attainder needed no evidence at all.
Somerset's original charges were so weak Northumberland had to retry him on the lesser charge of felony  -  that tells us something important about the strength of the case.
Confessions from condemned prisoners were often written by others and read aloud as the price of a less painful death.
These documents tell us what the government needed people to believe, not what the accused actually did.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was to blame for political instability?
examples.attribution: Proceedings in Parliament, 17 January 1549 [Act of Attainder against Thomas Seymour]
examples.excerpt: In the first year of King Edward's reign, the Lord Protector bears witness that the admiral, out of his great pride and ambition, would have seized control of his Majesty, to the King's peril and the overthrow of the state. The admiral wrote secretly to Parliament to stir up disloyalty, and bribed members of the Privy Chamber to conspire with him to depose the Protector, appoint a new council and arrange the King's marriage. The admiral disobeyed advice and sought to marry Princess Elizabeth, second in line to the throne, for which treasons he is imprisoned in the Tower.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view that the Seymour brothers' rivalry created political instability.
This is an Act of Attainder drafted by Somerset against his own brother. Parliamentary attainder required no evidence and no trial.
'Pride and ambition' and 'overthrow of the state' is the maximum case Somerset needed to make to justify executing Thomas.
The 'Lord Protector bears witness' line is Somerset using his official position to give evidence in a process he himself controlled.
The source tells us how Somerset chose to destroy his brother in 1549, not what Thomas Seymour had actually done.
knowledge: On Thomas Seymour's 'great pride and ambition' - he had courted Edward, married Katherine Parr, and was suspected of plotting to seize the King. The case had political logic, but Parliamentary attainder needed no evidence.

On Somerset acting against instability - executing his own brother in January 1549 set a 'dangerous precedent of faction leading to execution of an enemy'. The same precedent would be used against Somerset himself three years later.

On the Seymour rivalry as evidence of political instability - the events expose the structural problem of Edward's minority: powerful uncles competing for influence over a child king with no strong royal presence to balance them. Henry's Regency Council solution had already collapsed by 1547.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Somerset was to blame for / responsible for his own downfall?
examples.attribution: Parliamentary record of charges made against the Duke of Somerset, January 1552
examples.excerpt: Northumberland feared Somerset as the only person who might take away his control of the King. The duke planned to charge Somerset with treason for assembling men to kill him. The Lords debated but would not find Somerset guilty of any charge except 'conspiring to imprison Northumberland'. Several lords thought it unfit that Northumberland should himself give his verdict because the actions were against him, but it was agreed that a peer of the realm could not be challenged. After great debate, they all acquitted Somerset of treason, but a majority found him guilty of felony and condemned him to death.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view. The Lords would not convict Somerset of treason.
This is the parliamentary record of Somerset's trial. Tudor treason trials usually confirmed an outcome already decided, so the Lords' refusal here is significant.
Northumberland had to retry Somerset on the lesser charge of felony to get an execution. The original case was so weak even a sympathetic court would not accept it.
'Northumberland feared Somerset as the only person who might take away his control of the King' is the source itself naming the political motive for the prosecution.
The source is strong evidence that the case against Somerset in 1551-52 was constructed for political reasons by Northumberland, not because of genuine treason.
knowledge: On the Lords refusing to find Somerset guilty of treason - the evidence suggests the charges against Somerset were fabricated to remove him as a rival to Northumberland. The Lords' refusal to convict on treason confirms the political construction of the case.

On 'Northumberland feared Somerset as the only person who might take away his control of the King' - this is the source itself identifying the political motive. Somerset had been allowed back on the Council in the hope he would support Northumberland; the relationship broke down when Northumberland saw him as a continuing threat.

On the conviction for felony - this was a 'dangerous precedent of faction leading to execution of an enemy'. The same political logic would shape Northumberland's own execution after Mary's accession the following year.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition?
examples.attribution: Chelmsford Justices of the Peace, letter to Bishop Bonner, 27 April 1555
examples.excerpt: In our opinion he is one of the most arrogant heretics that hath been heard speak, or ever came before you, and not fit to be kept here in any jail, as well for fear of corrupting others, as for various and sundry other special causes hereafter to be more declared.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of opposition to the burnings, showing local officials enthusiastically pushing heresy prosecutions.
These are Essex JPs writing to Bishop Bonner. They are conservative Catholics taking the regime's policy seriously.
The framing of the prisoner as 'arrogant' and dangerous to others is the standard government language for justifying harsh treatment.

JPs were the local face of regime policy. Their enthusiasm is genuine but unrepresentative of the wider population. A Protestant labourer in the same village might have written a very different letter.
The source is good evidence of how the regime's policy was enforced locally in conservative areas, but it cannot stand for popular opinion as a whole.
knowledge: On the JPs calling the prisoner 'one of the most arrogant heretics' - by April 1555 the burnings had begun (Rogers, February). Essex was one of the Protestant strongholds where burnings would be concentrated. The JPs are local conservatives within the geographic heart of Protestant resistance.

On 'fear of corrupting others' - the regime's whole strategy assumed visible burnings would deter, not radicalise. Foxe's later Book of Martyrs would show this was mistaken. The JPs are echoing a regime line that turned out to be wrong.

On reading JP enthusiasm as evidence of popular support - Essex saw significant Protestant flight; around 800 Protestants had fled abroad by early 1554. JPs were the local face of regime policy, not a cross-section of opinion.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the succession never seriously threatened political stability?
examples.attribution: Lady Jane Dudley, letter to Queen Mary I, August 1553
examples.excerpt: The Duke of Northumberland announced King Edward's death. He said the King had considered it treason to acknowledge Mary, Your most serene Majesty, or Lady Elizabeth, as true heirs of the Crown. One disobeyed her father on religion and both were bastards. King Edward disinherited them and ordered the Council to obey. The duke said King Edward had named me the true heir. The Council kneeled before me, saying they would obey King Edward's wishes on pain of death. I was amazed and troubled, overcome by sudden grief and fell to the ground, weeping very bitterly. I resolved never to consent to my husband becoming King.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of a serious succession threat, presenting Jane as an unwilling pawn.
Jane was writing to Mary while a prisoner in the Tower. She was writing to save her life.
Presenting herself as overcome by grief and amazement deliberately shifts blame onto Northumberland. Whether she really felt this is unknowable.
This is also a religious appeal. Jane is positioning herself as a victim of Northumberland's ambition, not as Mary's enemy.
The source tells us what a prisoner needed Mary to believe about her role in the succession crisis, not whether she was genuinely as passive as she claims.
knowledge: On Jane's claim that Northumberland forced the succession - Northumberland did orchestrate the plot, marrying Jane to his son Guildford Dudley in May 1553 and keeping Edward's death secret for two days. Jane's account of being pushed is consistent with that.

On Jane being 'overcome by sudden grief' - Jane was 16 and writing from the Tower as Mary's prisoner. The presentation is calculated to position herself as Northumberland's victim. Mary did initially show leniency to many opponents, and the letter is shaped to that audience.

On reading this as 'no serious threat' - the affair required military mobilization, resulted in multiple executions, and exposed how a determined faction could attempt to seize the throne. Mary's leniency in resolving it does not mean the threat had not been real.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary's government was weak and divided?
examples.attribution: Sir Nicholas Throckmorton, evidence given at his trial for treason, 1554
examples.excerpt: I did see the whole realm was against it [the marriage] and although I counselled caution and urged restraint on those who would do mischief, it is I who is brought here before you. My Lords, in no wise am I guilty of treason because it was no treason to talk against the coming hither of the Spaniards.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view of a weak and divided government, with prominent figures openly criticising the Spanish marriage.
This is Throckmorton's defence at his own treason trial. He had every reason to present himself as a moderate voice rather than a conspirator.
The claim that 'the whole realm was against' the marriage is a defence strategy. He needed to normalise his own views as widespread, not subversive.
He was acquitted, which is rare in Tudor treason trials. That acquittal itself is the most striking piece of evidence about the political mood.
The source is strong evidence that opposition to the Spanish marriage extended into government circles, but Throckmorton's framing is shaped by his immediate need to save his life.
knowledge: On 'the whole realm was against' the marriage - the marriage triggered Wyatt's Rebellion, with 3,000 men and Norfolk's troops deserting. There was real and widespread opposition. Throckmorton is not inventing this, but he is using it as a defence.
On Throckmorton's acquittal - this was rare in Tudor treason trials. The acquittal itself shows there was significant elite sympathy with opposition to the marriage, even among judges.

On reading this as evidence of weak government - despite the rebellion, Mary proceeded with the marriage on the agreed treaty terms. The Council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign' and 'successfully carried out her wishes'. Internal opposition was vocal but contained.

sources.name: Churchwarden Accounts
sources.whatIsIt: Parish financial records  -  spending on church upkeep, buying Bibles, whitewashing images, restoring rood screens.
prompts: Written by local officials doing their administrative duty  -  not making theological statements.
Their value is in their mundanity. Written to record spending, not to persuade. When a parish records whitewashing images, that is real behaviour  -  not just an intention.
Never read belief from compliance. A churchwarden who buys a Protestant Bible under Edward and restores a rood screen under Mary is following the law.
They reveal huge regional variation. London looked very different from Cornwall  -  be careful about national generalisations.
These are the most direct evidence we have of what actually happened at parish level, rather than what the government wanted to happen.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the religious changes of Edward and Mary were welcomed at parish level?
examples.attribution: Illustrative churchwarden accounts in the style of an East Anglian parish, 1547-1555
examples.excerpt: 1547: Paid for the taking down of the rood and the whitening of the church walls by King's order, vij shillings. 1548: Paid for an English Bible chained at the lectern, xviij pence. 1549: Paid to John Cookes for the safe keeping of the silver chalice and silver pyx, iij shillings. 1551: Paid to the parish clerk for reading the new Prayer Book at the Sundays and Holy Days, xii pence. 1554: Paid for setting up again the high altar and for the cleaning of the chalice and pyx, v shillings. 1555: Paid for the painter to make new the rood loft and the figures thereon, xx shillings.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of welcome. The careful keeping of the chalice and pyx in 1549 shows a parish that complied outwardly with Edward's reforms but kept Catholic equipment ready in case the changes were reversed.

Churchwarden accounts were written to record spending, not to make theological statements. The neutrality of the form is what makes them so useful for showing what parishes actually did rather than what they said.
The reappearance of the chalice and pyx in 1554 and the restoration of the rood in 1555 suggests the parish never really committed to the Protestant changes.
The entry to John Cookes for safe keeping in 1549 is the most telling: this was a parish that expected the Reformation to be reversed.
The source is excellent evidence of parish-level pragmatism, but a single parish's accounts cannot tell us how representative this pattern was.
knowledge: On 'safe keeping of the silver chalice and silver pyx' in 1549 - de facto change under Edward was patchy. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia. Many parishes removed images when required but continued private Catholic devotion.

On 'setting up again the high altar' in 1554 - Catholic worship returned speedily across the country under Mary. Most church records identify Catholic practice resumed within months of Mary's accession, and people were 'willing to spend their minimal funds' on restoration.

On reading this as evidence of universal welcome - the parish complied with both regimes. Bishop Hooper's visitations of Gloucester found 171 of 311 clergymen could not even repeat the Ten Commandments. Compliance at parish level often reflected pragmatism more than belief, on both sides of the Reformation.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Reformation was welcomed in London and the south-east?
examples.attribution: Illustrative churchwarden accounts in the style of a London parish, 1547-1558
examples.excerpt: 1547: Paid to John Smith and his man for the taking down of the rood and the breaking of the high altar, xviij shillings. Paid for the painter to whiten over the wall paintings of saints, vj shillings. 1548: Paid for the English Bible chained at the lectern, ij shillings. 1551: Paid for the new communion table and a fair cloth for the same, viij shillings. 1552: Paid for the Second Book of Common Prayer for the use of the parish, iij shillings. 1554: Paid to set up a temporary altar as required by the bishop's officer, ij shillings vj pence. 1556: Paid to the painter for the figure of the rood, viij shillings; we had no money for the loft. 1558: Paid for cleaning and storing the communion table for safe keeping.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The parish removes the rood, whitens the wall paintings, buys the Bible and the prayer book promptly under Edward, and restores Catholic equipment under Mary only at the minimum required.
This is one London parish's spending record over eleven years. Churchwarden accounts were written to track money, not to make statements about faith, which is what makes them so useful.
The contrast with parishes in the north and west could not be sharper. The fast Edwardian compliance shows what was possible where reform had genuine local backing.

The Marian restoration entries are revealing. The 'temporary altar' of 1554, the rood figure with no loft in 1556, and the storing of the communion table in 1558 all suggest minimal grudging compliance, not enthusiasm.
The source is strong evidence of London's Protestant character, but London was the most Protestant area in the country. A single London parish cannot stand for England.
knowledge: On the speed of Edwardian compliance - de facto change under Edward was patchy nationally, but London, the south-east and East Anglia were the strongholds where Protestant change took hold most fully. Evidence from wills supports this geographical pattern.

On the minimal Marian restoration - around 800 Protestants fled abroad by early 1554, many of them from London. Those who stayed often complied with Mary's restoration outwardly while waiting for the regime to end.

On the 1558 'storing of the communion table' - Mary died on 17 November 1558. A parish storing rather than destroying its communion table was preparing for a swift Elizabethan reversal, which came in 1559.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that there was widespread enthusiasm for the Catholic restoration under Mary?
examples.attribution: Illustrative churchwarden accounts in the style of a Lancashire parish, 1554-1558
examples.excerpt: 1554: Paid for the setting up of the high altar with new linen, x shillings. Paid to William the carver for the figure of Our Lady and Saint John for the rood loft, xxvi shillings viij pence. 1555: Paid for the great banner of the patron saint, used in procession, xv shillings. Paid for new candles before the rood and at the altar of Our Lady, iv shillings. 1556: Paid to the players of the Corpus Christi play, xii shillings. Paid to the priest for the trental of the souls of those parishioners deceased without proper rites under the late king, x shillings. 1557: Paid for the visitation by my Lord Cardinal's officer and for the banquet of the same, xxx shillings. Paid for the gilding of the chalice and the new pyx, xviij shillings.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The parish is spending substantial sums on rood figures, banners, candles, the Corpus Christi play, and even retrospective masses for those who died under Edward. This is investment, not compliance.

These are routine financial records of one Lancashire parish, but the scale and choice of expenditure are themselves the most useful evidence. Money for the Corpus Christi play and the priest's banquet at the visitation are choices, not requirements.
The entry for the trental for parishioners who died under Edward 'without proper rites' is unusually revealing. The parish was paying retrospectively to make good what it saw as a religious wrong.
The northwest was the most conservative part of the country. Lancashire churchwarden accounts of this kind would look very different from London accounts of the same period.
The source is strong evidence of genuine Catholic enthusiasm in one Lancashire parish, but the regional contrast with London means this cannot be used to claim national enthusiasm.
knowledge: On the parish spending substantial money on restoration - Catholic worship returned speedily across the country, and in the North and West restoration was 'welcomed rather than merely accepted'. Lancashire fits the geographical pattern of strongest enthusiasm.
