On the trental for those who died under Edward - this implies belief in purgatory and the efficacy of masses for the dead, which Protestants rejected. Retrospective masses suggest the parish saw Edwardian religion as a temporary disaster they were now correcting.

On the Corpus Christi play - the great medieval mystery plays had largely been suppressed or fallen away under Edward. Their revival under Mary signalled real local Catholic life, not just official compliance with the Royal Injunctions of 1554.

sources.name: Visitation Records
sources.whatIsIt: Records of bishops inspecting parishes  -  checking equipment, services, and whether clergy were teaching correctly.
prompts: Written by bishops and their officials  -  reflects the priorities of church authority, not ordinary parishioners.
Standard questions produce standard answers. This creates a false impression of uniformity across very different parishes.
Non-compliance recorded here is some of the best evidence for the gap between what reform intended and what it actually achieved.
The view from above. Tells us what bishops were looking for, not what ordinary people experienced.
Parishes learned to give the right answers. Compliance recorded here often means a parish that knew what its bishop wanted to hear, not one that had actually reformed.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was resistance and opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: Archdeacon Harpsfield's Visitation, 1557 [Canterbury diocese parishes ordered to fit out churches for Catholic worship]
examples.excerpt:
The Church of Goodnestone
First, front cloths for the altar for the holidays and a canopy and veil against Lent.
The reparations as tiling and glazing to be done upon the Chancel at the said Michaelmas and the reparations needful to be done at the said feast.

The Parish Church of Goudhurst
To repair the glass windows of the church before All Saints.
Also, that the window in the belfry be glazed before Midsummer, and to be closed otherwise decently so that no pigeons may come into the church.
That the vicarage house to be repaired.
That the churchyard to be enclosed decently.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of resistance, showing parishes complying with Catholic requirements for liturgical equipment.
Visitation records were produced by bishops and their officials. They reflect what the church authorities were looking for, not what parishioners actually felt.
The fact that these items had to be ordered in 1557, four years into Mary's reign, suggests the parish was behind on the basic equipment needed for Catholic worship.
Visitations work to a standard checklist. Parishes learn the right answers to give. Compliance recorded here often means a parish that knew what the visitor wanted to hear.
The source is more useful as evidence of the gap between Catholic policy and parish reality in Kent in 1557 than as evidence of genuine religious revival.
knowledge: On items being ordered in 1557 - Mary's reign had begun in 1553. The Royal Injunctions of 1554 had restored traditional Catholic practices, and the Second Act of Repeal had reversed all post-1529 religious legislation. The fact that basic equipment still needed ordering four years in shows that restoration at parish level was a slow practical process.

On the parish's compliance - the wider picture is that Catholic worship returned speedily and people were 'willing to spend their minimal funds' on restoration. Even in Protestant areas like Kent, parishes returned to Catholic practice without visible opposition.

On reading this as evidence of resistance - over 800 clergy were deprived for failing to return to Catholic practice, but this was clerical resistance rather than parish revolt. Mary's restoration was 'more successful than the Edwardian Reformation had been'; the slowness in particular parishes shows the gap between policy and patchwork local implementation, not opposition.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Edwardian Reformation was difficult to enforce in practice?
examples.attribution: Illustrative visitation findings in the style of Bishop Hooper's visitation of the diocese of Gloucester, 1551-52
examples.excerpt: The Vicar of Bisley: Could not repeat the Lord's Prayer in English. Said that he had been ordained under King Henry and was now too old to learn. The parish: The altar yet standing as it had been. No communion table provided. The English Bible chained at the lectern but the parishioners cannot read it and the priest does not read from it. The Rector of Dursley: Could repeat the Lord's Prayer but did not know who was the author of it. The parish: The wall paintings whitened over by command, but the rood loft yet standing with the figures hidden behind a curtain.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The findings record clerical ignorance, parishes ignoring the order to replace altars, hidden Catholic equipment, and Bibles that go unread.
Visitation records were produced by bishops and their officials, not by ordinary parishioners. They reflect what church authorities were looking for: equipment, services, clerical knowledge.

The format of findings against named parishes and priests was the standard administrative tool of Tudor religious enforcement. The records exist because the bishop wanted leverage to improve compliance.
Bishops who were committed reformers would compile findings that showed how far there was to go. A more conservative bishop in the same diocese might have recorded the same parishes very differently.

The source is strong evidence of widespread non-compliance with Edwardian reform in one diocese in 1551-52, but the bishop's choice of what to investigate and how to record it shapes the picture as much as the parishes' actual practice.
knowledge: On the vicar who could not repeat the Lord's Prayer - Bishop Hooper's actual visitation of Gloucester in 1551 found 171 of 311 clergymen unable to repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 unable to find the Lord's Prayer in the Bible. Clerical ignorance was a structural obstacle to Protestant reform, not an isolated problem.

On 'the altar yet standing' - the order to replace altars with communion tables had gone out by 1550. Two years later, parishes were still resisting. Evidence from churchwarden accounts confirms that altars were often the last thing to be removed.

On the rood loft figures hidden behind a curtain - this fits a pattern of parishes complying outwardly while keeping Catholic equipment in case the regime changed. The speed of restoration under Mary in 1553-54 confirms that much of this hidden equipment came back into use very quickly.

sources.name: Wills
sources.whatIsIt: Legal documents recording last wishes, including religious preambles that can indicate Catholic or Protestant beliefs. Survive in very large numbers.
prompts: A wealthy merchant dictating their own will is a very different source from a labourer whose parish priest wrote it for them. The agency of the testator matters enormously.
Religious preambles read as personal belief. In reality, the same phrasing appears across dozens of wills written by the same scribe. The surface is intimate. The reality is often formulaic.
Were testators writing their own words, or repeating phrases the scribe suggested? The two are very different things.
Most students only see a handful of examples. That is not enough to draw conclusions from.
Religious preambles can reflect genuine belief, legal convention, or simply whatever formula the local clergyman offered.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that traditional Catholic beliefs remained strong in northern England under Edward VI?
examples.attribution: Illustrative will of a Yorkshire husbandman, proved 1551
examples.excerpt: In the name of God, Amen. I, Robert Hodgson of the parish of [X], husbandman, being whole of mind and remembrance, do make this my last will. First, I bequeath my soul unto Almighty God my Maker and Redeemer, and to Our Blessed Lady Saint Mary, and to all the saints and holy company of heaven, trusting through their intercession to be saved. My body to be buried within the churchyard of my said parish. I give unto my parish priest to sing a trental of masses for my soul, vj shillings viij pence. I give unto the high altar of my parish church for tithes forgotten, xij pence. I give to the poor men of the said parish, that they pray for me, iij shillings. The residue of all my goods, after my debts and funeral expenses are paid, I give to my wife Margaret, whom I make my sole executrix.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The invocation of the Virgin Mary and the saints, the trust in their intercession, the trental of masses paid for, the bequest to the high altar, and alms to the poor for prayers all signal unmistakably Catholic belief.
But this is the will of one Yorkshire husbandman in 1551, almost certainly drafted by his parish priest. The wording reflects the scribe's preferred formula more than Hodgson's personal theology.
The same phrases appear across dozens of wills written by the same scribe in the same parish. What looks intimate is often formulaic legal language imposed by the priest at the bedside.

The specific bequests reveal a parish openly ignoring central reform. The trental of masses had been outlawed in principle by the dissolution of the chantries in 1547, and high altars had been ordered replaced with communion tables in 1550.

The source is strong evidence of continuing Catholic practice in one Yorkshire parish in 1551, but a handful of wills cannot stand for a whole region, and the formula does not necessarily reflect Hodgson's own beliefs.
knowledge: On 'Our Blessed Lady Saint Mary' and 'the saints and holy company of heaven' - invocation of the Virgin and the saints, and the doctrine of saintly intercession, were core Catholic beliefs that Protestants rejected. In Yorkshire and the north, traditional religion remained strong under Edward. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia.

On 'a trental of masses for my soul' - paying a priest to say masses for the dead implied belief in purgatory, which Protestants rejected. The chantries had been dissolved in 1547 partly to eliminate this practice. Conservative parishes ignored the dissolution and continued these formulas in wills well into Edward's reign.

On 'the high altar of my parish church' - altars had been ordered replaced with communion tables by 1550. The formula continues here in 1551, which shows the parish dragging its feet on central reform. This was common in the north and west, where de facto compliance with the Edwardian Reformation was patchy.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Edwardian Reformation had transformed religious belief among ordinary English people?
examples.attribution: Illustrative will of a London merchant, proved 1551
examples.excerpt: In the name of God, Amen. I, Thomas Marsh of the parish of St Mary Aldermary in the City of London, mercer, being of whole and perfect mind, do make this my last will and testament. First, I bequeath my soul unto Almighty God my Maker and my only Saviour Jesus Christ, by whose precious blood alone I trust to be saved, and to no creature nor saint, and my body to be buried without pomp or candle in the churchyard of my said parish. I will that no dirge nor month's mind be kept for me, but that the cost thereof be given to the poor. I bequeath to my apprentice John Walker two English Bibles, that he may read them and instruct his household. The residue of my goods I leave to my wife Joan, whom I make my sole executrix, charging her to bring up our children in the true knowledge of God's Word.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The will rejects saintly intercession explicitly, refuses Catholic funeral rites, redirects funeral expenses to the poor, and bequeaths English Bibles. The Protestant theology is unmistakable.

This is the will of one London merchant in 1551. Merchants tended to be more literate, more independent of parish clergy, and more likely to have dictated their own words than husbandmen further from the capital.

The explicit rejection of saints and funeral rites is unusual. Most Protestant wills of this period are less direct, often using the formula 'trusting through Christ alone' without naming what is being rejected. Marsh's wording is unusually emphatic.

St Mary Aldermary was in the heart of the City of London, the most Protestant area in the country. The audience for this will, including the parish priest who would witness it, would have been broadly sympathetic.

The source is strong evidence of committed Protestant belief in one London merchant in 1551, but London was the most Protestant area in England, and a wealthy merchant's will is not typical of how ordinary people made their bequests.
knowledge: On 'to no creature nor saint' - this explicit rejection of saintly intercession was core Reformed theology. Evidence from wills shows that London, the south-east and East Anglia were the strongholds where Protestant ideas took genuine hold. This will fits the geographical pattern.

On 'no dirge nor month's mind' - dirges and month's mind masses were Catholic practices for the souls of the dead. Their explicit rejection here goes further than most Protestant wills of the period, which often simply omit such requests rather than forbid them.

On the bequest of two English Bibles - the English Bible had been chained in every parish church under Henry VIII's 1538 injunction and confirmed under Edward. By 1551 English Bibles were widely available in London, but their use in family instruction marks Marsh as an actively practising Protestant, not just a passive conformist.

sources.name: Edward VI's Chronicle
sources.whatIsIt: Edward VI's personal journal from around 1549  -  recording council decisions, rebellions, and religious change in a terse, factual style.
prompts: Written by a boy raised by Protestant humanist tutors. His view of events reflects their values as much as his own.
Presented as a private diary, but the formal style and likely audience suggest it was always intended to be read. Almost certainly meant to demonstrate Edward's capability as a future ruler.
After 1549, Edward's information came largely through Northumberland. He is probably repeating Northumberland's version of events without questioning it.

After 1549, Edward's information and framing came largely through Northumberland. The Chronicle reflects Northumberland's dominant narrative  -  Somerset is condemned without sympathy, Protestant reform is presented as inevitable progress. What is absent is as telling as what is present.
Edward never questions Northumberland's actions or the pace and purpose of the Reformation. That absence of doubt is itself revealing.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the gentry and nobility were responsible for the unrest in 1549?
examples.attribution: Edward VI's Journal, 1549
examples.excerpt: The people rebelled in Sussex, Hampshire and Kent, where, by fair persuasions, partly from honest men among the rebels, and partly by local governors, they were satisfied and went home. After that, the people rose in Oxfordshire, the West Country and Norfolk. The marquis of Northampton was sent to Norwich, with 1060 horsemen, but lost 100 men in battle and retreated. The earl of Warwick replaced him, with 7500 men, and fought the rebels for three days in Norwich before overcoming them outside the city, killing 2000 of them. The Council gathered in London, to charge Protector Somerset with allowing these rebellions to occur.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of gentry and nobility responsibility, presenting the people as the agents of rebellion and the local governors as the ones restoring order.
Edward was 12 in 1549 and almost entirely dependent on Northumberland and his tutors for his understanding of events. He was not making independent observations.
His information about the rebellions came through Northumberland, who had defeated Kett and was about to remove Somerset. Edward records the version that suited Northumberland.
The entry is terse and factual in style, which makes it sound objective. But the choice of what to record is shaped by his sources at court, not by the rebels themselves.
The source tells us what the young king at Westminster understood about the 1549 rebellions, not whether the gentry were really to blame.
knowledge: On the rebels being 'satisfied and went home' - this fits the Privy Council's preferred narrative that the unrest was being managed. The reality was over 25 counties in unrest, 16,000 rebels at Kett's Norwich camp, and a Western Rebellion that took 8,000 troops to suppress.

On the rebellions being settled 'by fair persuasions' - Kett's rebels were ultimately massacred at Dussindale: 3,000 killed and 49 leaders executed. Over 3,000 Western rebels were executed after Sampford Courtenay. The persuasions were not fair.

On the framing as 'the people' rising against 'local governors' - Edward's framing puts blame on the commons. But Lord Sheffield was beaten to death at Norwich and Bodmin rebels chanted 'Kill all the gentlemen!' The rebellions targeted gentry specifically, suggesting gentry behaviour was at least part of the cause.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that religion was the most serious cause of division between Edward's government and Mary in 1551?
examples.attribution: Edward VI's Chronicle, entry for 18 March 1551
examples.excerpt: The Lady Mary, my sister, came to me at Westminster, where after salutations she was called with my Council into a chamber where it was declared to her how long I had suffered her mass against my will, and how I was now resolved that her mass should no longer be celebrated. She answered that her soul was God's and her faith she would not change, nor she would not dissimulate her opinion with contrary doings. To this I said I would not constrain her faith, but I willed her not as a king to rule but as a subject to obey. After much discourse she went away. Her servants who had said her mass were ordered to be committed to the Tower.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. Edward records his half-sister Mary defying his religious authority in person, with her servants imprisoned as a direct consequence.

Edward was 13 when this entry was written. The framing of the exchange (Mary called before 'me' and 'my Council') presents the king as the active centre, which Northumberland's regime needed him to appear.

The Chronicle was written in Edward's own hand but the political framing reflects Northumberland's preferred narrative. By 1551 Edward's information about court politics came almost entirely through Northumberland and his tutors.

The wording given to Mary ('her soul was God's') is dignified and theological, but the wording given to Edward ('not as a king to rule but as a subject to obey') is the regime's preferred line on Mary's status as Edward's subject.
The source is good evidence of the regime's view of the Mary-Edward religious dispute, but the framing reflects Northumberland's preferred presentation as much as Edward's independent judgement.
knowledge: On Mary's defiance - Mary's commitment to the Catholic mass was the central religious issue of her relationship with Edward's government. Her position as next in line under Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession meant she could not be set aside easily, which made her defiance politically dangerous.

On her servants committed to the Tower - the regime targeted Mary's household priests rather than Mary herself, which was the limit of what they could safely do. Mary's status as heir constrained the government's options.

On reading this as evidence of serious division - the religious dispute was real, but it was Edward and Northumberland's response to it (drafting the Devise for the Succession in 1553 to exclude Mary altogether) that turned a continuing tension into a constitutional crisis.

sources.name: The Devise for the Succession
sources.whatIsIt: A document in Edward's handwriting trying to pass the crown to Lady Jane Grey  -  altered from 'Jane's male heirs' to 'Jane and her heirs male'.
prompts: Edward was a dying teenager surrounded by powerful men with strong reasons to stop a Catholic succession. Genuine belief and political manipulation are not mutually exclusive.
Presents itself as a sovereign act of royal will. In reality, the king is fifteen and dying, surrounded by men who need him to write what they need him to write.
Northumberland signed it knowing it would keep him in power. His self-interest shapes the whole document.
Who changed the wording from 'Jane's male heirs' to 'Jane and her heirs male'? Edward, Northumberland's agents, or someone after Edward's death? Never settled.
The handwriting dispute means we cannot even be certain what Edward himself wrote versus what was added later.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that female rule was a serious problem in the 1550s?
examples.attribution: Letters Patent for the limitation of the Crown, 21 June 1553
examples.excerpt: As Lady Mary and Lady Elizabeth are both illegitimate they have no claim to the crown. As half blood to us, they would be barred by ancient law and custom of this realm and could not succeed us even if legitimate. Were the said Mary or Elizabeth to have the crown of England and marry a foreigner, he would practise his own country's laws and customs within this realm. This would utterly subvert the commonwealth of this our realm. We therefore declare that the crown shall, for lack of issue of our body, come firstly to the eldest son of Lady Frances Grey or, secondly, to the Lady Jane and her male heirs.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view, since the Devise treats female rule plus a foreign marriage as so dangerous that the established succession has to be set aside.
Edward was 15 and dying. The Devise was drafted in the months before his death in July 1553, by a king completely dependent on those around him.
Northumberland had every reason to support the Devise. Mary's accession would mean the end of his power and the restoration of Catholicism. He signed it knowing it kept him in control.

The argument that a foreign marriage 'would utterly subvert the commonwealth' is a legal pretext for excluding Mary specifically. The willingness to make Jane Grey queen shows female rule itself was not the real objection.
The source tells us what Northumberland and a dying teenage king needed people to accept about the succession, not whether female rule itself was the constitutional problem they claimed.
knowledge: On the foreign marriage clause - the actual marriage treaty negotiated for Mary and Philip in 1554 restricted Philip from holding office, prevented English involvement in Spain's wars, and gave Mary total control of offices and revenues. The 'subversion of the commonwealth' the Devise predicts is the danger the treaty was carefully designed to prevent.

On Lady Jane Grey as the alternative - Northumberland strengthened his grip by marrying Jane to his son Guildford Dudley in May 1553. The Devise was as much about keeping Northumberland in power as preventing Catholic succession.

On reading this as evidence of the female rule problem - the willingness to make Jane Grey queen actually shows gender mattered less than religion. The objection was specifically to Mary, not to female rule in principle.

sources.name: The Books of Common Prayer
sources.whatIsIt: Cranmer's Prayer Books  -  the deliberately vague 1549 version and the clearly Protestant 1552 revision.
prompts: Written by Cranmer, an expert on religious language who knew exactly how to be deliberately ambiguous. Expertise is not the same as objectivity.
Official religious texts  -  telling us what the government wanted people to believe, not how congregations responded.

On the surface, a single national church. Underneath, the 1549 wording on the Eucharist is so ambiguous that Catholics and Protestants could both attend the same service while believing entirely different things about what was happening.
Compare 1549 and 1552 side by side. The removal of almost all Catholic ceremony in 1552 shows how fast the Reformation was actually moving.
The Western Rebellion was directly triggered by the 1549 Prayer Book. The source and the resistance it caused must be read together.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the religious changes under Edward were intended to be moderate in 1549?
examples.attribution: Illustrative rubric in the style of the 1549 First Book of Common Prayer
examples.excerpt: When the minister delivereth the bread to the people, he shall say: The Body of our Lord Jesus Christ which was given for thee, preserve thy body and soul unto everlasting life. And the people shall receive standing, or kneeling as they have been accustomed, as the bishop in his discretion shall appoint. Let nothing be done that giveth scandal to the weaker brethren or that may seem to overthrow the customs of the Church too suddenly.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view, with explicit instructions to avoid scandalising parishioners and to allow customary practice.
The 1549 Prayer Book was written by Cranmer, an expert in religious language who knew exactly how to make doctrine deliberately ambiguous.
Phrases like 'as the bishop in his discretion shall appoint' do important political work, leaving local practice flexible while giving the impression of a single national church.
The compromise was designed so that both Catholics and Protestants could attend the same service while believing different things about what was happening.
The source tells us about the regime's strategy in 1549, a careful first step intended to look moderate while preparing the ground for further change.
knowledge: On 'standing, or kneeling as they have been accustomed' - the 1549 Prayer Book was a deliberate compromise that 'pleased nobody'. Its ambiguity on the Eucharist directly triggered the Western Rebellion in early 1549, with over 3,000 rebels executed.

On 'nothing be done that giveth scandal' - the moderation was tactical. By 1552, with Northumberland in power, the Second Prayer Book removed almost all Catholic ceremony and confirmed Calvin's purely symbolic doctrine. The moderation of 1549 was a stepping stone, not the end point.

On 'the bishop in his discretion shall appoint' - at parish level, evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia. The flexibility built into the 1549 settlement allowed parishes to drag their feet.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that by 1552 the Edwardian Reformation had moved decisively in a Protestant direction?
examples.attribution: Illustrative rubric in the style of the 1552 Second Book of Common Prayer
examples.excerpt: When the minister delivereth the bread, he shall say to every one severally: Take and eat this in remembrance that Christ died for thee, and feed on him in thy heart by faith with thanksgiving. And the minister that delivereth the cup shall say: Drink this in remembrance that Christ's blood was shed for thee, and be thankful. And the people shall receive the same kneeling. Such ornaments of the church and of the ministers thereof at all times of their ministration as were retained under King Edward in the second year shall be taken away.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The Communion wording is now memorial and symbolic, the ornaments of the 1549 version are removed, and the theological compromise of three years earlier is gone.

The 1552 Prayer Book was drafted by Cranmer at the height of Northumberland's regime, when Protestant reformers had unprecedented influence at court. The text reflects what was now politically possible.
The new wording ('in remembrance' rather than 'the body of our Lord') confirms Calvin's purely symbolic doctrine of Communion. This was a deliberate doctrinal choice, not a stylistic preference.
The removal of ornaments retained in 1549 ends the visual compromise that had allowed both Catholics and Protestants to attend the same service while believing different things.
The source is strong evidence of how far the regime's Protestant vision had advanced by 1552, but the text tells us what the regime intended for parishes, not how parishes received it.
knowledge: On the memorial language - this is Calvin's purely symbolic doctrine, the most radical Reformed position on the Eucharist. The change from 1549 marks the moment when the Edwardian Reformation moved beyond ambiguity into clearly Reformed theology.

On the removal of ornaments - the 1552 settlement also brought the Second Act of Uniformity, threatening six months in prison for non-attendance. Both moves reflect the regime's confidence that it could push much harder than in 1549.

On reading this as decisive Protestantism - Edward died in July 1553, less than a year after the 1552 Prayer Book came into use. The Forty-Two Articles were drafted in 1552 but never passed by Parliament. The decisive shift was on paper; whether it had time to embed at parish level is a separate question.

sources.name: The Edwardian Homilies
sources.whatIsIt: Twelve sermons issued by royal authority in 1547, to be read aloud in churches  -  written because clergy could not be trusted to preach the new theology themselves.
prompts: Produced by the Edwardian government  -  an official statement of what the regime wanted every English person to believe.
The fact these were needed shows how little the government trusted parish priests in 1547. That itself tells us something important about the state of the clergy.
Far more theologically direct than the 1549 Prayer Book  -  different documents, different audiences, different strategies.
Tells us what the government wanted people to believe about salvation and scripture. Not whether they believed it.
Use visitation records and churchwarden accounts alongside  -  they show whether the homilies were actually being read in churches.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Edwardian government sought to introduce Protestant doctrine clearly and directly?
examples.attribution: Illustrative extract in the style of the Edwardian Book of Homilies, 1547 (Homily on Justification)
examples.excerpt: Whoever therefore believeth in Christ shall be saved, and not by his own works, nor by any merits of his own, but by the free mercy of God in Jesus Christ alone. Let no man think that good works are not necessary, for good works do follow true faith as fruit follows the tree. But it is faith alone, and not any work of man, that maketh us righteous before Almighty God. This doctrine doth not destroy good works, but rather establish them, for he that loveth God will keep His commandments.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The doctrine of justification by faith alone, with works as a fruit not a cause of righteousness, is unambiguously Protestant.
This is an official text issued by royal authority in 1547. It tells us what the regime wanted parishioners to be taught, not what they actually understood or believed.

The Homilies were written precisely because parish clergy could not be trusted to preach the new theology themselves. The very existence of an official sermon to be read aloud reflects clerical ignorance and resistance.
Compare the directness here with the deliberately ambiguous wording of the 1549 Prayer Book on the Eucharist. The Homilies and the Prayer Book were doing different jobs for different audiences.

The source tells us what the Edwardian government wanted English people to believe about salvation in 1547. Whether the sermon was actually read in every parish, and whether listeners absorbed its theology, is a separate question.
knowledge: On 'faith alone... maketh us righteous before Almighty God' - this is justification by faith, the central Protestant doctrine. Its inclusion in the Homilies from 1547 shows the regime was prepared to teach core Reformed theology directly from the start.

On the need for an official sermon to be read aloud - Bishop Hooper's visitations of Gloucester found 171 of 311 clergymen could not repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer. The Homilies existed because clergy could not be trusted to preach the new doctrine themselves.

On reading the Homilies as evidence of effective religious change - de facto change at parish level was patchy. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia. The clarity of the Homilies cannot tell us how clearly they were being received.

sources.name: The Zurich Letters
sources.whatIsIt: Letters between English Protestant reformers and theologians in Zurich  -  especially Heinrich Bullinger  -  reporting on the English Reformation.
prompts: Committed Protestant reformers writing to their theological heroes abroad. They had every reason to present England positively.
Letters between allies  -  achievements are emphasised, setbacks ignored. They construct the picture of England that reformers wanted Bullinger to see.
Not truly private  -  writers knew letters could be intercepted. They wrote with that in mind.
Reformers had real access to events but filtered everything through a Protestant lens that assumed reform was right and necessary.
They never question the pace or purpose of the Reformation  -  only complain it is moving too slowly. That one-sidedness is the point.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was widespread opposition to religious changes under Edward VI?
examples.attribution: Sir John Cheke, letter to a Protestant reformer in Switzerland, 1553
examples.excerpt: The king has accomplished more in his youth than many have done in their adult life. He has repealed the Act of Six Articles. He has removed images from churches. He has overthrown image worship. He has abolished the mass and destroyed almost every kind of superstition. He has published good and pious homilies to lessen the ignorance of uneducated ministers. Each of these achievements would be considered a great action in other men, but as nothing to him, given the very great amount he has accomplished.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view of widespread opposition. Cheke presents the Edwardian Reformation as a series of triumphs.

Cheke was Edward's tutor. The opening line - 'more in his youth than many have done in their adult life' - lets the tutor take credit through his pupil. The praise of the king is also self-praise, and his reasons to celebrate are personal as well as religious.
He was writing to a Protestant ally in Switzerland. Letters between reformers were a form of mutual encouragement, where achievements were emphasised and setbacks ignored.
His list of accomplishments is real (Six Articles repealed, images removed, the mass abolished) but it is told as a story of forward progress, not as a record of how it was received.
The source tells us how committed Edwardian reformers wanted the Continental Protestant network to view the English Reformation, not how the country actually received it.
knowledge: On 'the Six Articles' being repealed - this happened in 1547, opening 'a Pandora's box of radical ideas' as Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all preached openly. The repeal was more chaotic than triumphal.

On images being removed and the mass abolished - de jure England was Protestant by 1553, but de facto compliance was patchy. Bishop Hooper found 171 of 311 clergymen in Gloucester could not repeat the Ten Commandments.

On the achievement being 'in his youth' - Edward died in July 1553. The Second Prayer Book and Forty-Two Articles came only in the final months. Cheke's celebration covers a Reformation that had barely had time to embed.

examples.paper: Guide Source Practice / Y107 past papers
examples.question: How far do they support the view that the introduction of Protestantism under Edward VI was difficult?
examples.attribution: Martin Bucer, letter to John Calvin, June 1550 [German Protestant theologian, taught at Cambridge]
examples.excerpt: The Bishops have not yet agreed on Christian doctrine, let alone the rules of the Church, and very few parishes have qualified clergymen. Sometimes the clergy read the service rapidly, so that the ordinary people have no more understanding of it than if it were still in Latin rather than English.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of difficulty, listing very specific problems with bishops, clergy and Parliament.
Bucer was a German Protestant theologian teaching at Cambridge, brought in to support the Reformation. He had high expectations of how it should work in practice.
His complaints are detailed because he was an insider trying to push reform forward, frustrated at the slow pace. He was writing to Calvin to pressure the regime through the Continental network.
His remedy is to urge Somerset to do more, which fits the wider pattern of reformers complaining the Reformation was not moving fast enough.
The source is strong contemporary evidence of practical obstacles to Protestant reform, from a committed reformer who wanted it to succeed.
knowledge: On 'very few parishes have qualified clergymen' - Bishop Hooper's visitations of Gloucester found 171 of 311 clergymen could not repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer. Clerical ignorance was a real structural obstacle.

On the clergy reading the services 'rapidly' so people did not understand - this was happening in English by 1550, but de facto change was patchy. Evidence from wills shows little support for Protestant changes outside London, the south-east and East Anglia.

On urging Somerset to push reform - Somerset fell from power in October 1549 (Bucer's letter was June 1550, before Northumberland's rise was complete). The pace of reform did accelerate from 1550 once Northumberland took over.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary's restoration of Catholicism was popular?
examples.attribution: John Jewel, letter to Henry Bullinger, 20 March 1559 [Protestant bishop, former Marian exile]
examples.excerpt: Our universities are so depressed and ruined that at Oxford there are scarcely two individuals who think with us. Some despicable friars have reduced the vineyard of the Lord into a wilderness. You would scarcely believe that so much desolation could have been effected in so short a time.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view that Mary's restoration had been popular, by describing the universities under Mary as ruined.
Jewel was a Protestant bishop and a former Marian exile, writing only months after Elizabeth's accession in 1558.
His audience is Bullinger in Zurich, the centre of the exiles' Continental network. The letter is part of building the Elizabethan case for renewed Protestant reform.
His description of Oxford as 'depressed and ruined' with 'despicable friars' is rhetorical Protestant framing of the Marian university. It expresses a partisan view of what restoration meant.
The source tells us how a returning Marian exile presented Mary's restoration to his Continental allies in 1559. It is not a measured assessment of how popular Catholic restoration had been.
knowledge: On Oxford being 'depressed and ruined' - over 800 clergy were deprived during Mary's reign for refusing to return to Catholic practice. Catholic restoration was 'more successful than the Edwardian Reformation had been', particularly in conservative areas.

On 'despicable friars' reducing the universities - this is exile rhetoric. The 12 Decrees of 1556 had aimed at clerical reform: bans on absenteeism, pluralism and simony. The Marian Church was not simply degraded.

On Marian restoration as ruin - the fact that Elizabeth needed her own Reformation, with significant time required to re-establish Protestantism, suggests Mary's regime had actually been more successful at the local level than Jewel admits.

sources.name: Kett's Rebellion Articles
sources.whatIsIt: Twenty-nine formal demands from Kett's Rebellion in Norfolk, 1549  -  focused on economic grievances like enclosure and excessive rents.
prompts: The careful legal drafting shows this was written by gentry, not ordinary Norfolk peasants. Kett himself was a landowner.
Formal written demands  -  presenting the rebels as loyal subjects with legitimate grievances, not troublemakers.
Shows that ordinary people engaged with national politics in more sophisticated ways than we might expect.
No religious demands at all. The contrast with the Western rebels' articles is the most important thing about this source.
The gentry leadership shaped what grievances were articulated. Ordinary rebels may have had different or additional concerns that never made it into the articles.

examples.paper: Guide Unit 3 Source Practice / Y107 past papers
examples.question: How far do they support the view that the main cause of rebellions 1547-58 was religion?
examples.attribution: Five of the twenty-nine Articles drawn up by Robert Kett, July 1549
examples.excerpt:
1. We pray your grace that from now on no man shall enclose any more.
8. We pray that ministers that cannot preach God's Word be dismissed, and replaced by others, chosen by the parishioners or lord of the town.
14. We pray that land that is unreasonably rented may be priced as in 1485, and that when lands change hands, the fees are easy to pay.
15. We pray that every priest shall reside in his parish so his parishioners may be taught God's laws.
16. We pray that all bondmen may be made free, for God made all free with his precious blood.
provenance: On the surface the articles are dominated by enclosure (1) and rents (14), with religion limited to clerical reform (8, 15). The religious content is Reformed-leaning (preaching clergy, resident priests), the opposite of the Western Rebellion's demand for Catholic restoration in the same year.

The careful petition format - 'We pray your grace' - is gentry-drafted legal language, not the voice of ordinary Norfolk peasants. Kett himself was a landowner. The framing presents the rebels as loyal subjects with legitimate grievances.
Article 14's reference to 1485 land prices shows precise historical knowledge - the start of the Tudor dynasty. This is literate, planning rebellion, not a spontaneous mob.

Article 16's theological argument - 'God made all free with his precious blood' - justifies social demands with explicitly Reformed scripture. This is the same scriptural reasoning radical reformers were making across Europe.
Only five of twenty-nine articles are given here. The full set might emphasise other themes differently. This is a curated selection; we cannot read the rebellion's full priorities from it.
knowledge: On 'no man shall enclose any more' - this was Kett's central demand. The 16,000 rebels gathered around enclosure and high rents. In Norwich 6% of the population owned 60% of the land. The economic grievance was concrete and measurable.

On 'ministers that cannot preach God's Word be dismissed' - Bishop Hooper's visitations of Gloucester found 171 of 311 clergymen could not repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer. The clerical complaint here matches a documented national problem.

On 'land that is unreasonably rented may be priced as in 1485' - rising population (2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551) had pushed rents sharply up. The article asks for pre-Tudor levels, framing the demand as restoration rather than radicalism.

On 'all bondmen may be made free, for God made all free with his precious blood' - this is one of the most theologically radical demands of any Tudor rebellion. It uses Reformed scripture to justify social equality, the opposite framing of the Western Rebellion which used Catholic worship to legitimise resistance.

sources.name: The Western Rebels' Articles
sources.whatIsIt: Demands from the Western (Prayer Book) rebels of 1549  -  calling for the Latin Mass, Six Articles, and traditional Catholic practice.
prompts: Written by conservative clergy, not ordinary Cornish and Devon people. The church leadership shaped what this rebellion was about.
Formal demands presenting rebels as loyal subjects  -  but the clergy were using the commons to fight their own battle.
Many Western rebels didn't speak English and had no opinion on Reformed theology. The clergy were speaking for them  -  and for themselves.
Compare directly with Kett's Articles. One rebellion is about religion, one about economics. That contrast is central to understanding 1549.
The rebels called the new Prayer Book 'a Christmas game'  -  the voice of educated clergy, not ordinary farmers.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that there was widespread opposition to religious changes under Edward VI?
examples.attribution: The demands of the Western rebels, 1549
examples.excerpt:
Item, we will have the Laws of our Sovereign Lord King Henry VIII concerning the Six Articles, to be in use again, as they were during his reign.
Item, we will have the mass in Latin, as it was before, and celebrated by the priest without any man or woman communicating with him.
Item, we will have holy bread and holy water every Sunday, palms and ashes at the accustomed time, Images set up again in every church.
Item, we will not receive the new service because it is like a Christmas game, but will have our old service of Matins, mass, Evensong and procession in Latin.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of opposition, with explicit demands for Latin mass, the Six Articles, and rejection of the new Prayer Book.
The demands were drawn up by literate local clergy, not by ordinary Cornish and Devon people. The rebellion's religious framing was the clergy's, even where the rebels' real grievances were broader.
Many of the rebels in Cornwall spoke Cornish rather than English. They had no theological position on Reformed doctrine, but they did know that the new service was unfamiliar.
Calling the new service 'like a Christmas game' is the voice of educated clergy ridiculing what they saw as theatrical innovation.

The source is strong evidence that the clergy who shaped the rebellion framed it religiously. It is less reliable as evidence of what ordinary rebels thought, where wider grievances about taxes, rents and gentry power were also present.
knowledge: On 'we will have the mass in Latin' - the Western Rebellion was triggered specifically by the First Book of Common Prayer enforced in early 1549. Many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English, so the new service felt alien on both religious and linguistic grounds.

On 'we will have the Laws... concerning the Six Articles' - the Six Articles (Henry VIII's Catholic doctrine) had been repealed in 1547. The rebels' demand for their return is a clear reversal of the Edwardian Reformation.

On reading this as a purely religious rising - at Bodmin the rebels chanted 'Kill all the gentlemen!' Earlier demands included high taxes and rents. The rebels' real motives were broader than the clergy's drafted articles allow, and the brutal government response (over 3,000 executed) shows how seriously the regime took both dimensions.

sources.name: Commonwealth Writers
sources.whatIsIt: Protestant writers like Robert Crowley and Thomas Lever who attacked enclosure, rack-renting, and the exploitation of the poor in Edward's reign.
prompts: Educated Protestant preachers writing for wealthy, literate audiences  -  not for the poor they were describing.
Moral campaigners, not neutral observers. Their descriptions of poverty are vivid but deliberately shaped to shame the powerful into action.
Writing during a period of real economic hardship  -  their anger reflects genuine anxiety even if the detail is overstated.
Protestant social criticism directed upward, toward those with power  -  not outward toward the commons themselves.

They never admit that Protestant religious reform itself might be causing popular unrest. Their social criticism operates entirely within a Protestant framework  -  they are constructing a narrative in which economic suffering has a moral cause (greedy landlords) rather than a structural one. This is itself a dominant narrative.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that price inflation was the main cause of unrest in 1549?
examples.attribution: Thomas Becon, The Jewel of Joy, 1547-48 [chaplain to Protector Somerset]
examples.excerpt: See how landlords, especially sheep owners, oppress the king's subjects by enclosing the common pasture and filling it with their sheep. How many sheep they have! Yet when was wool so expensive or mutton so great a price? If this goes on, the people will die of cold or starve to death. For these greedy wolves will either sell their wool and their sheep at their own high prices, or else not at all.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view that inflation and economic grievance were behind the 1549 unrest, with greedy sheep-owning landlords as the villains.
Becon was chaplain to Protector Somerset. His criticisms reflect Somerset's own preferred explanation: blame the gentry, not government policy.
He is writing as a Protestant social critic, not as an economist. The emphasis on the moral failings of landlords lets him explain hardship without confronting the structural causes of inflation.
His audience is wealthy and literate, the very people he is attacking. The aim is to shame them into action, not to give a neutral diagnosis.
The source is good evidence of how Edwardian Protestant social criticism framed economic hardship, but the framing serves a political argument rather than describing the causes accurately.
knowledge: On 'how many sheep they have' - enclosure had picked up pace because of the growing cloth market in the Netherlands. Gentry were transforming agricultural land to livestock, producing less food and requiring fewer farm hands. The grievance Becon describes was real.

On 'when was wool so expensive or mutton so great a price' - food prices had doubled since the start of the century. The Great Price Rise was driven by inflation, debasement (Somerset's own policy), and population pressure rising from 2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551.

On blaming landlords for high prices - the Commonwealth writers like Becon did not understand the real causes (debasement, bullion from the New World, population pressure). Blaming greedy landlords was morally satisfying but economically wrong.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that price inflation was the main cause of unrest in 1549?
examples.attribution: Hugh Latimer, Sermon, preached in 1550
examples.excerpt: You preachers, I urge you to speak against greed and to criticise those great men and men of power who oppress the poor. For greed is the cause of rebellion. Greed was the cause of rebellion last year, by both gentlemen and common people. The people thought they had the right to things they desired. The gentlemen wanted to keep what they had, so they rebelled or disobeyed the king's orders. Thus both sides were greedy, and both sides rebelled.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view that greed and inflation drove the 1549 rebellions, with both gentlemen and commoners blamed.
Latimer was one of the most prominent Protestant preachers of the day, a senior figure in the Edwardian Reformation. His sermon is a moral diagnosis of rebellion, not an economic one.
Preached in 1550, in the immediate aftermath of the previous year's risings, his sermon is part of the broader Commonwealth writers' project of pinning the unrest on personal greed.
His call to preachers to attack the powerful echoes the Edwardian regime's preferred explanation: the rebellions were a moral problem, not a failure of policy.
The source tells us how leading reformers wanted the 1549 rebellions to be understood. It is less useful as evidence of what actually caused them.
knowledge: On 'greed was the cause of rebellion last year, by both gentlemen and common people' - 1549 saw the most widespread unrest of the Tudor period, with over 25 counties affected. The scale was real, even if Latimer's diagnosis was moral rather than structural.

On preachers being urged to criticise the powerful - the Commonwealth writers were preaching to wealthy literate audiences. Their criticism worked within a Protestant framework that blamed personal greed rather than the structural problems of inflation and debasement.

On reading 'greed' as the cause - 1549 was driven by inflation, population pressure (rising from 2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551), debasement, and bad harvests linked to the Little Ice Age. Greed was a symptom of economic dislocation, not its origin.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the gentry were responsible for unrest / that price inflation was the main cause?
examples.attribution: Robert Crowley, The Way to Wealth, 1550
examples.excerpt: Rebellion is a dangerous disease and its causes must be rooted out. If I should ask a poor man what is the cause of rebellion, he will blame the great farmers, lawyers, gentlemen, knights and lords. Men of greed. Men who take our houses from us and enclose our commons. If I should ask these greedy men what is the cause of rebellion, they will say that the peasants are too wealthy, they are disobedient, they would destroy gentlemen. They will try again to compel the king to grant their requests, and will be punished for it, as happened last year.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view that gentry responsibility, especially around enclosure and rents, was central to the 1549 unrest.
Crowley was a leading Commonwealth writer, attacking those who profited from the dissolution of the monasteries and the booming wool trade.
His list of specific grievances (enclosure, higher entry fees, raised rents) is detailed and largely accurate. The grievances did exist.

But his entire framing assumes the cause of suffering is gentry greed rather than structural inflation, debasement, or population pressure. That moral framing was the Commonwealth writers' political project.
The source is good evidence of contemporary Protestant criticism of the gentry, but it consistently misses the wider economic forces that the Commonwealth writers did not understand.
knowledge: On 'enclosed from the poor their common land' - Kett's 16,000 rebels in Norfolk gathered explicitly around enclosure and rents. In Norwich, 6% of the population owned 60% of the land. The gentry behaviour Crowley attacks was documented.

On 'levied greater entry fees... raised their rents' - rising population (2.3 to 3 million between 1525 and 1551) created huge demand for land, allowing landlords to charge more. The actions Crowley describes are correctly observed, but the underlying cause is demographic, not moral.

On laying responsibility on the gentry - this misses that Spain's New World silver was flooding European markets, debasement (Somerset's policy) reduced confidence in the currency, and harvests were failing because of the Little Ice Age. Gentry behaviour worsened things but did not cause them.

sources.name: Foxe's Acts and Monuments
sources.whatIsIt: John Foxe's martyrology published 1563, recording Protestant persecution under Mary. Under Elizabeth, every parish was ordered to display it alongside the Bible.
prompts: A Protestant exile writing to legitimise his faith by casting its followers as heroic martyrs. Every editorial choice serves that argument.
Ordered into every parish under Elizabeth  -  state-sponsored Protestant propaganda that tells us as much about Elizabeth's reign as Mary's.

Ask whether this is a source about Mary's reign or about how Elizabethan Protestants needed Mary's reign to be remembered. Foxe was constructing a dominant Protestant narrative  -  the idea that England was always a Protestant nation temporarily corrupted by a Catholic queen. That narrative had enormous political uses under Elizabeth.
Some accounts are second or third hand, already shaped by earlier retellings before they reached Foxe.
When Foxe records hostile crowds or difficult deaths, those details are probably accurate  -  they damage his own argument, so he had no reason to include them.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments ('The Book of Martyrs'), 1563
examples.excerpt: On his way to St. Albans there was a great gathering of people to see and hear the prisoner; some were very sorry to see so godly a man brought to be burned. There were, however, some who said it was a pity he did stand in such opinions; and others, both old women and men, cried against him; one called him 'heretic', and said it was a pity that he lived. But George Tankervil did speak to them so effectually that God softened their hardened hearts, so that some of them departed with weeping eyes.
provenance: On the surface this supports the view that the burnings created opposition, with sympathetic crowds and a martyr framing.
Foxe was a Protestant exile during Mary's reign, writing his Acts and Monuments under Elizabeth and publishing in 1563.
The book was ordered to be displayed in every parish church under Elizabeth, making it state-sponsored Protestant propaganda for an Elizabethan as well as a Marian audience.
The detail of the crowd being 'softened' by Tankervil's words fits the martyrology structure: holy man, hostile world, divine vindication. Every scene is shaped by that argument.

The source tells us how Elizabethan Protestants needed the Marian burnings to be remembered. Where Foxe records hostile or mixed crowds at burnings, those details are probably reliable because they damage his own argument.
knowledge: On the 'great gathering of people' at the burnings - this matches contemporary reports. Large crowds did attend the burnings, but there is little evidence they converted the audience to Protestantism; many treated burnings as entertainment.

On Tankervil's words 'softening' hardened hearts - this is the martyrology structure at work. Even where Foxe records crowds containing both sympathy and hostility, his framing always closes with vindication. The structure shapes every scene.

On reading Foxe as evidence of widespread opposition - 284 Protestants were burnt over three years. Cranmer, Ridley, Latimer and Hooper were eliminated. The exiles' printing presses kept Protestant works in circulation (19,000 copies of the Second Prayer Book survive). Foxe's later reach matters: under Elizabeth, every parish was ordered to display his Book of Martyrs.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition to Mary's religious policies?
examples.attribution: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments, account of the burning of Bishops Latimer and Ridley at Oxford, 16 October 1555
examples.excerpt: Doctor Ridley and Master Latimer were brought forth to the place of execution. When they came to the stake, Master Latimer ran to it and embraced it. They were both stripped to their shirts. The fire was kindled. Then Master Latimer spake unto Master Ridley these words: 'Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man. We shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.' Master Latimer received the flame with both his hands, and bathing his face with it, gave up the ghost. Master Ridley, by reason of the evil making of the fire, was long in burning, but at length the flame burst forth and consumed him.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view. The scene is constructed as martyrdom: dignified bishops, defiant words, a 'candle' that will never go out, all witnessed before a crowd at Oxford.
Foxe was a Protestant exile during Mary's reign, writing under Elizabeth and publishing in 1563. Every editorial choice serves the argument that Mary's victims were holy martyrs.

The Latimer speech was probably real in substance but is unlikely to have been recorded exactly as Foxe gives it. Martyrology depends on memorable last words, and Foxe's text became their standard form.

The detail of Ridley's slow burning 'by reason of the evil making of the fire' is the kind of detail Foxe includes because it intensifies the martyrdom rather than undermining it. The suffering becomes the proof.

Under Elizabeth, Foxe's Acts and Monuments was ordered into every parish church. This scene was being recited as scripture by 1570. The source tells us how the burnings were remembered as much as how they happened.
knowledge: On the burning of Latimer and Ridley at Oxford - the burnings began with John Rogers in February 1555 and continued until Mary's death in 1558, with 284 Protestants burnt in total. Latimer and Ridley were among the most senior figures. Cranmer would follow in March 1556.

On the 'candle in England' speech - even if Foxe sharpened the wording, the broader Protestant cause did survive Mary's reign. Around 800 Protestants had already fled abroad by early 1554, and their printing presses kept Cranmer's Prayer Book and other Reformed works in circulation across Europe.

On the public reaction - large crowds did attend the burnings, but contemporary evidence is mixed about how they responded. Some viewed burnings as entertainment, some as religious atrocity. Foxe's narrative focuses on the moments of sympathy, which fits his argument but cannot stand alone as a measure of national feeling.

sources.name: Renard's Diplomatic Dispatches
sources.whatIsIt: Letters from Simon Renard, the Spanish ambassador, to Charles V and Philip II  -  covering Mary's court, the Spanish marriage, and crises like Wyatt's Rebellion.
prompts: A Spanish diplomat advancing Habsburg interests  -  not a neutral observer. He highlighted threats and opportunities that mattered to Spain.
Diplomatic dispatches written to impress his masters and protect his career. Crises are over-reported, stability ignored.

Trapped in a Spanish bubble  -  his contacts shared his anxieties, making him prone to overestimating threats like Wyatt's Rebellion. He also had unusual personal influence over Mary, meaning he was shaping events, not just reporting them.
Repeatedly misread English politics  -  overestimated the Protestant threat, underestimated noble loyalty to Mary.
When he reports something damaging to his own case  -  like English hostility to Philip  -  that detail is probably true. He had every reason to leave it out.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the Marian burnings created opposition?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, report to Philip of Spain, 5 February 1555
examples.excerpt: The people of London are murmuring about the cruel enforcement of the recent acts of Parliament against heresy which has now begun, as shown publicly when a certain Rogers was burnt yesterday. Some of the onlookers wept. Others prayed to God to give them strength, persistence, and patience to bear the pain and not to convert back to Catholicism. Others gathered the ashes and bones and wrapped them up in paper to preserve them. Yet others threatened the bishops. The haste with which the bishops have proceeded in this matter may well cause a revolt. If the people got the upper hand, not only would the cause of religion be again menaced, but the persons of your Majesty and the Queen might be in peril.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view, suggesting the burnings were creating real public anger in London.
Renard was a Spanish ambassador with a vested interest in Mary's regime succeeding. He has no reason to invent opposition.
But Renard's job was to flag risks to his masters in Brussels. He tended to dramatise threats because that was what kept him useful.
'May well cause a revolt' is his speculation, not a fact. His informants were close to him in London. He was not watching the burnings in other parts of the country.
The source is good evidence of London hostility to the first burnings in early 1555. The talk of 'revolt' reflects Renard's instinct to flag danger, not necessarily reality.
knowledge: On 'the people of London are murmuring' - the burnings were concentrated in London, Kent and Essex, the Protestant strongholds. Renard's report of London anger matches the geographical reality.
On 'may well cause a revolt' - no popular revolt followed. The burnings continued for nearly three more years, ending only with Mary's death in 1558. Renard's predicted danger never materialised.

On the early-stage reaction - Renard is writing about the first major burning (John Rogers, 4 February 1555). Gardiner was still alive and opposed the burnings as counter-productive. Mary had already advised the Council in December 1554 to act 'without rashness', showing regime awareness of the risk.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary Tudor's government was weak?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, letter to Charles V, 18 September 1554
examples.excerpt: No attention is paid to the law; the Queen and her council are neither respected nor obeyed nor feared. The people say that King Philip is not going to employ Englishmen, though he agreed to do so in the marriage treaty. They (the people) say he is sending for 10000 Germans and 10000 Spaniards to land in this country. They also say that monasteries will be set up again and that the Pope will control religious affairs. They proclaim that they (the people) are to be enslaved, for the Queen is a Spanish woman at heart and thinks nothing of Englishmen.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of weakness.
Renard's job was to flag problems for Philip and the Emperor. Crises were over-reported in his dispatches because that was what kept him useful.
'The people say' covers his London contacts, who were anxious about the Spanish marriage. It is not a measured assessment of national opinion.
He had personal influence over Mary and reasons to argue that her regime needed continued Spanish support. Painting things as bleak helped that case.
The source is evidence of Renard's view of the autumn 1554 mood. It is not a reliable measure of how weak Mary's government actually was.
knowledge: On 'neither respected nor obeyed nor feared' - Mary had defeated the Jane Grey coup in nine days, suppressed Wyatt's Rebellion personally, and negotiated a marriage treaty that significantly restricted Philip's power. Her record by autumn 1554 cuts against Renard's bleak framing.

On 'King Philip is not going to employ Englishmen' - the marriage treaty explicitly forbade Spaniards holding office in England. Mary kept total control of all offices, lands and revenues. The popular rumour Renard reports was unfounded.

On the wider regime - Mary streamlined the Council and her inner council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign' and 'successfully carried out her wishes'. Renard's snapshot of one moment of anxiety is not the whole picture.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Wyatt's rebellion was a serious threat to Mary?
examples.attribution: Simon Renard, dispatch, 27 January 1554
examples.excerpt: Wyatt's men have rebelled in Kent, proclaiming that they will not consent to a foreign marriage and that every good Englishman ought to help them fight the Spaniards. Although the rebels use the foreign marriage as an excuse, like Carew, their real causes are religion and to favour Elizabeth. It is said that the rebellion is spreading. We hear news that the French and Scots are hastily fitting out ships and raising troops to aid the rebels. We hear the king of Denmark is joining in, hoping to marry Elizabeth to his son or brother.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view of a serious threat. Renard reports Kent in rebellion and warns of religion and Elizabeth as the real motives behind the stated complaint against the Spanish marriage.

Renard was writing from the middle of the Spanish contingent at court, who were genuinely frightened by Wyatt's advance on London. The dispatch reflects their anxieties, and he was asking Charles V for help in the same letters.

He had every reason to recast the rebellion as religious and pro-Elizabeth. That framing made the rebels look illegitimate and helped defend the Spanish marriage, which was the source of his own influence.

The hedging language gives him away. 'It is said' and 'we hear news' show he is passing on court gossip rather than verified intelligence. The escalating list of France, Scots, and even the King of Denmark joining in reads as the hyperbole of a frightened ambassador, not a measured report.
The source is genuine evidence of the alarm inside the Spanish bubble at court in late January 1554, not a reliable measure of the rebels' real motives or the rebellion's actual scale.
knowledge: On 'Wyatt's men have rebelled in Kent' - the rebellion raised 3,000 men and reached the gates of London. Government troops under Norfolk deserted to join the rebels, declaring 'We are all Englishmen!' Renard's alarm is not overstated.

On 'their real causes are religion and to favour Elizabeth' - the rebellion's timing immediately followed Mary's marriage proposal in Parliament, and Wyatt had been loyal to Mary during the Jane Grey affair. He only turned after the marriage was announced. Religion is the convenient reading, not the most likely cause.

On Renard's framing - Proctor's government-commissioned history also blamed religion, exactly because the regime could not afford to admit popular opposition to Philip. The Spanish ambassador and the regime's chronicler reach the same conclusion for the same reasons.

sources.name: The Venetian Ambassador Reports
sources.whatIsIt: Diplomatic reports from Venetian ambassadors to the Senate of Venice on Mary's reign and the Spanish marriage.
prompts: Venice had the most professional diplomatic service in Europe  -  trained observers sent to report accurately, not to advance a dynastic agenda.
No stake in English politics  -  less biased than Renard, but also less well connected to what was really happening at court.
Venice cared about Mediterranean trade and the European balance of power. That shapes what they noticed and what they ignored.
Most useful when read alongside Renard's dispatches  -  two observers from opposite sides interpreting the same events very differently. That contrast is the point.
Sober and professional in tone, which is the source's biggest danger. Their calm prose can read as reliable when they are simply reporting court gossip with better grammar than Renard.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary Tudor's government was weak?
examples.attribution: The Venetian ambassador, report to the Senate of Venice, 1557
examples.excerpt: She is not only brave and valiant, but so courageous and resolute that neither in adversity nor peril did she ever display cowardice, maintaining always a wonderful grandeur and dignity, knowing what suits the dignity of a sovereign as well as any of her experienced councillors. In government and public affairs she is compelled (being of a sex which cannot suitably take more than a moderate part in them) to refer many matters to her councillors and ministers. The truth is that knowing the divisions among them, her Majesty, so as not to be deceived, has ordered that Cardinal Pole should hear and have everything referred to him since she trusts him and distrusts almost all others.
provenance: On the surface this both supports and challenges the view. It praises Mary's courage but says she relies heavily on her councillors.
The Venetian ambassador had no direct stake in English politics. Venice valued accurate information for diplomatic decisions in the Mediterranean.
The professional and measured tone is the source's biggest danger. Calm prose makes it sound reliable, but the ambassador is still reporting court gossip and surface impressions.
The line about Mary being 'compelled' to refer to her councillors reflects assumptions about female rule shared across Europe in the 1550s. It is interpretation, not fact.
The source gives a balanced contemporary judgement on Mary's personal qualities, but it cannot tell us how her government was actually performing day to day.
knowledge: On Mary 'compelled... to refer matters to her councillors' - Mary did rely on her Council, but she streamlined it (casual councillors excluded from key committees in 1554; inner council established in 1555). The Council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign'.

On Mary's 'courageous and resolute' character - this matches her refusal to flee London during Wyatt's Rebellion, her personal Guildhall speech, and her willingness to push through Catholic restoration despite Council resistance. The personal qualities described are not just praise.

On the wider judgement - Mary 'in practice demonstrated that a woman could govern effectively'. She streamlined the Privy Council, passed major religious legislation, managed marriage negotiations, and suppressed Wyatt's Rebellion.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that Mary's restoration of Catholicism was popular?
examples.attribution: Giovanni Michiel, letter to the Senate of Venice, 13 May 1557
examples.excerpt: The Catholic religion seems daily to increase and take root, through the Queen's authority and the Cardinal's diligence. Monasteries are being built, churches are full, the ancient rites and ceremonies are again performed. But except for a few, most pretend to reject Protestantism and on the first opportunity would return to it.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view that the restoration was popular, since Michiel says most people would return to Protestantism on the first opportunity.
Michiel was a Venetian ambassador writing in May 1557, three and a half years into Mary's reign. He had no Habsburg axe to grind.
The cautious framing (most 'pretend to reject Protestantism') reflects court gossip and is hard for any outside observer to verify. He is reporting an impression, not a survey.

His underlying claim, that Catholic restoration was widely accepted but shallow, is the kind of judgement a Venetian ambassador could plausibly form from court contact but could not test in the parishes.
The source gives a thoughtful contemporary assessment that captures both the visible success of restoration and the suspicion that compliance was thin. The 'thinness' is interpretation, not evidence.
knowledge: On 'monasteries are being built, churches are full' - the visible signs of restoration were real. Catholic worship returned speedily across the country, with most parishes welcoming the return rather than just accepting it.

On 'most pretend to reject Protestantism and on the first opportunity would return to it' - around 800 Protestants had fled abroad by early 1554, and their printing presses kept Protestant works in circulation. The exiles would return as Puritan agitators under Elizabeth. Michiel's suspicion captured a real concern.

On the geography - in the North and West, restoration was genuinely 'welcomed rather than merely accepted'. Michiel's claim of widespread pretence reflects what court contacts told him about London and the south-east, where Protestant strongholds were concentrated, more than the country as a whole.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that enclosure was the most important cause of unrest in 1549?
examples.attribution: Matteo Dandolo, letter to the Senate of Venice, 20 July 1549
examples.excerpt: There is news of major risings against the government in England, and that the king has retreated to a strong castle outside London. The cause of this is the common land, as the great landowners occupy the pastures of the poor people. The rebels also require the return of the mass, together with the religion as it stood on the death of Henry VIII. The government, wishing to apply a remedy, put upwards of 500 persons to the sword, sparing neither women nor children.
provenance: On the surface this names common land first as the cause - placing enclosure ahead of the religious demands.
Dandolo was the Venetian ambassador, with no direct stake in English politics. Venice wanted accurate information for Mediterranean diplomacy.
'the king has retreated to a strong castle outside London' is factually wrong - Edward did not flee London. The error reveals Dandolo working from secondhand court reports, not direct observation.

The conflation of demands - common land (Kett's Rebellion in Norfolk) AND return of the mass (Western Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall) - shows Dandolo merging two distinct rebellions with very different causes. From London they look like one event.

'500 persons to the sword, sparing neither women nor children' is dramatising language and the figure is far too low. This is the kind of vivid touch ambassadors used to make crises memorable for their masters.
knowledge: On 'the common land, as the great landowners occupy the pastures of the poor' - Kett's 16,000 rebels gathered around enclosure and rents. In Norwich 6% of the population owned 60% of the land. The enclosure grievance Dandolo identifies was real.

On 'the rebels also require the return of the mass' - this is the Western Rebellion's demand, triggered by the First Book of Common Prayer. Dandolo is hearing about two different rebellions with very different causes and merging them into one.

On '500 persons to the sword' - the actual suppression was far larger. Warwick killed 3,000 at Dussindale alone; over 3,000 Western rebels were executed after Sampford Courtenay. Dandolo's figure dramatically understates the regime's violence.

On 'the king has retreated to a strong castle outside London' - this did not happen. The error reveals Dandolo's distance from the events. Useful evidence of how the 1549 crisis looked from outside England, not a reliable account of what occurred.

sources.name: The French Ambassador Dispatches
sources.whatIsIt: Reports from French ambassadors  -  especially Antoine de Noailles  -  to Henri II, covering the Spanish marriage and English politics.
prompts: French diplomats with a direct interest in destabilising England. Anything that weakened a Spanish-allied England served French interests.
De Noailles was in contact with Wyatt's rebels  -  he was not observing the rebellion, he was helping to cause it.
Most useful when read against Renard's dispatches. Same events, completely opposite agendas  -  the contrast reveals how national interest shapes what observers claim to see.
Well connected but deeply partisan. Their reports on English opposition to the Spanish marriage are likely exaggerated.
French pressure eventually helped drag England into the Habsburg-Valois war and the loss of Calais in 1558. These dispatches are part of that story.

examples.question: How far do these sources support the view that the Spanish marriage was unpopular with the English people?
examples.attribution: Illustrative French ambassadorial dispatch in the style of Antoine de Noailles, summer 1554
