examples.excerpt: The Spaniards are hated wherever they go in this kingdom. In London, members of the queen's Spanish household are insulted and stones are thrown at their lodgings. Merchants complain that English ships are no longer safe from the Emperor's fleet, and gentlemen who once spoke for the queen now murmur openly against the marriage. The queen herself is reported to be thin and unwell. If your Majesty wishes to weaken this country's tie to the Habsburgs, no better moment will come.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view, presenting universal hostility to the Spaniards across multiple sections of English society.
The dispatch is written by a French ambassador, whose explicit role was to weaken an England allied with Spain. The framing is shaped by French strategic interests.
French ambassadors of this period, especially Noailles, were in active contact with English opposition figures. They were not simply observing discontent, they were helping to organise it.
The closing line 'no better moment will come' reveals the purpose. This is intelligence written to argue for French intervention, not a measured report on public opinion.
The source is genuine evidence of what French diplomats believed about English opposition to the Spanish marriage, but the picture is shaped by their need to make the case for action.
knowledge: On 'the Spaniards are hated wherever they go' - opposition to the Spanish marriage was real and had triggered Wyatt's Rebellion in January 1554, with 3,000 men and Norfolk's troops deserting. But 'wherever' overstates the geography: opposition was concentrated in London and the south-east, not nationwide.

On 'gentlemen now murmur openly against the marriage' - Throckmorton's acquittal at his treason trial in 1554 confirmed elite sympathy with opposition to the marriage. But Mary's Council 'worked effectively together for most of her reign' and the marriage proceeded on the agreed treaty terms.

On the call for French intervention - the marriage treaty restricted Philip from holding office, prevented English entanglement in Spain's wars, and gave Mary total control of offices and revenues. By summer 1554 the political moment for French disruption had largely passed.

sources.name: Knox's First Blast of the Trumpet
sources.whatIsIt: A pamphlet by Scottish Protestant John Knox, published in Geneva 1558, arguing that female rule was against God, nature, and law. Aimed mainly at Mary I.
prompts: Knox was a powerful, charismatic Calvinist preacher with a zealous congregation behind him. His ideas were widely shared among committed Protestants  -  this was not just one man's view.
A carefully structured theological argument using scripture and classical authorities  -  designed to be difficult to argue against within the thinking of the time.
Written in Geneva because it could not safely be written in England. What could only be said from abroad tells us about the limits of free expression under Mary.
Knox was a Protestant exile with strong connections to the reforming network across Europe  -  well informed about the wider Protestant cause if not always about English politics specifically.
Backfired badly when Elizabeth became queen  -  she was furious. This shows Knox was speaking for a committed Calvinist fringe, not mainstream English Protestant opinion.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that female rule was a serious problem in the 1550s?
examples.attribution: John Knox, The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women, 1558
examples.excerpt: To promote a woman to rule a nation is unnatural and insulting to God as contrary to his revealed will and law. It is the subversion of good order and justice. No–one can deny that it is repugnant to nature that the blind shall lead those who can see, the weak protect the strong, or the foolish and mad govern the discreet and give counsel to those of sober mind. Such are all women compared to man in bearing authority. For as rulers, their sight is blindness; their strength, weakness; their advice, foolishness; and their judgement, frenzy.
provenance: On the surface this strongly supports the view, calling female rule unnatural and against God.

Knox was writing from Geneva in 1558, not England, because the pamphlet could not safely be written under Mary. That fact alone cuts against the view: if Mary's government was really that weak, he could have written it at home.
Knox was a Calvinist preacher writing for fellow Protestant exiles. He is not a neutral observer of English politics, he is a religious campaigner with strong views.
Most English Protestants actually accepted Mary as queen even when they disagreed with her religion. Knox spoke for a committed Calvinist fringe, not the mainstream.

When Elizabeth came to the throne just months after publication, the pamphlet backfired badly. The source tells us more about Knox's religious opposition to women rulers in general than about whether female rule was actually a serious problem in the 1550s.
knowledge: On 'unnatural and insulting to God' - Mary actually demonstrated that a woman could govern effectively. She streamlined the Privy Council, passed major religious legislation, managed the Spanish marriage on tightly restrictive terms, and suppressed Wyatt's Rebellion personally.

On female rule as 'subversion of good order' - the willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen showed gender was seen as less important than religion even within Protestant circles. Knox represents a fringe Calvinist position, not mainstream Protestant thinking.

On the pamphlet's reception - Knox published in 1558, but Elizabeth came to the throne months later. She was furious, and the pamphlet damaged Knox's standing badly. The work that was meant to undermine female rule ended up confirming that radical Calvinism was politically marginal in England.

sources.name: Wyatt's Rebel Documents
sources.whatIsIt: Manifestos and proclamations from Wyatt's rebellion of 1554  -  a Kent-based rising against the Spanish marriage.
prompts: Written by rebel leaders trying to build the broadest possible coalition. The language had to be unifying, not divisive.
Manifestos are designed to win support  -  the stated cause was opposition to the Spanish marriage, not Mary's religion. A Protestant rebellion would have attracted far fewer people.
Mary needed it to look like a religious plot to justify her response. Wyatt needed it to look constitutional to maximise support. Both sides had reasons to misrepresent it.
The rebellion nearly succeeded  -  Mary only held London after her personal speech at the Guildhall. That near-success shows how fragile her position really was.
The documents never mention Protestant motivation  -  even though it almost certainly existed. That deliberate omission is itself the most important thing about them.

examples.question: How far do they support the view that the main cause of rebellions was religion?
examples.attribution: Sir Thomas Wyatt, proclamation to the people of Kent, January 1554
examples.excerpt: We write to you as friends, neighbours and Englishmen, concerning Queen Mary's declared intention to marry a foreigner, and request you to join us to prevent this. We swear to you before God that we seek no harm to the Queen, but merely wish her better advice. Our wealth and health depend on it.
provenance: On the surface this challenges the view that religion was the main cause of rebellions in this period. The proclamation focuses entirely on the foreign marriage.
This is a rebel leader's public manifesto, designed to attract the broadest possible support in Kent. The language has to be unifying, not divisive.
Wyatt was himself a Protestant, but he knew that a religious appeal would attract far fewer recruits than xenophobic opposition to the Spanish marriage. The omission of religion is deliberate.

Calling the rebels 'friends, neighbours and Englishmen' is the same nationalist appeal the regime's own forces would later turn on Wyatt when government troops under Norfolk deserted to him declaring 'We are all Englishmen!'
The source tells us how the rebel leadership chose to frame the rebellion. Whether religion was the real underlying motive is precisely what the proclamation is constructed to disguise.
knowledge: On 'concerning Queen Mary's declared intention to marry a foreigner' - the timing of the rebellion (immediately after Mary proposed the marriage in Parliament) supports the marriage as the real trigger. Wyatt had been loyal to Mary during the Jane Grey affair.

On 'we seek no harm to the Queen' - despite this disavowal, part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth, who would defend Protestantism. The proclamation's restraint is rebel strategy, not actual intention.

On 'friends, neighbours and Englishmen' - this xenophobic framing was the most effective recruiting tool the rebels had. Religion would have attracted far fewer recruits. The proclamation omits religion deliberately, but Wyatt and many leaders were themselves Protestant, and Kent was a Protestant area with trading links to Northern Europe.
